Mass Deportation Coalition

Mass Deportation Coalition Playbook

March 30, 2026

Promises Made

Introduction

What’s At Stake: The Necessity of Mass Deportation

As the United States of America completes her 250th year of existence, the central question for the people of this nation is whether they desire to preserve a sovereign nation, composed of a self-governing people organized through the Constitution and with a government with fidelity to the rule of law.

After decades of sustained illegal immigration and little enforcement, the consequences facing our nation are no longer theoretical. State and local governments are carrying an unsustainable fiscal burden as public services are extended to those who should not be here and their dependents. What was once understood as a limited safety net for citizens has, in practice, been stretched into a parallel system for non-citizens. Through a combination of emergency mandates, administrative loopholes, and widespread abuse, billions of taxpayer dollars are diverted each year to sustain this reality. Estimates vary, but analyses of federal and state expenditures suggest that total public costs associated with this foreign invasion run into the hundreds of billions annually, according to the Federation for American Immigration Reform. In many cases, access to benefits is facilitated through fraudulent documentation, identity manipulation, or the exploitation of mixed-status households; often with the knowing assistance of individuals and advocacy networks willing to subordinate the interests of American citizens to an ideological agenda.

Hospitals and emergency services, particularly in border states and urban centers, operate under increasing uncompensated care burdens, with costs ultimately borne by taxpayers. Federal law compels hospitals to provide emergency care regardless of legal status, contributing to tens of billions of dollars in uncompensated care nationwide each year, according to data from the American Hospital Association. In border states and major urban centers, this has become a persistent and growing burden, forcing hospitals to shift costs onto taxpayers and insured patients while reducing capacity for the communities they were built to serve. Emergency services have left local governments to cover costs that are never recovered.

America is not facing a temporary challenge. Public systems designed to serve the American people are being repurposed, without consent and without limit, to sustain foreigners. Further, the steady degradation of service quality and a growing fiscal crisis at the state and local level are culminating in an increasingly justified belief among American citizens that their government is failing in its most basic obligation: to serve its own people first.

At the same time, the labor market effects are not evenly distributed. While aggregate economic indicators such as GDP growth or overall employment may obscure localized impacts, the burden falls heavily on lower-income American workers, particularly those without college degrees, who compete in sectors of the economy where wages are being compressed. Economic research has consistently shown that increases in the supply of low-skilled foreign labor place downward pressure on wages for similarly situated native workers. This is especially true in industries such as construction, restaurants, hospitality, agriculture, and manufacturing, according to the Center for Immigration Studies. Even modest wage suppression, when compounded over time, has significant consequences for American families living paycheck to paycheck.

This dynamic reinforces economic immobility for working-class Americans. Workers have lost the ability to adjust. Employers, faced with a larger labor pool, have gained an illicit leverage to suppress native-born wages, reduce benefits, and bypass labor standards. This influx has contributed to a bifurcation of the labor market. For working-class Americans, particularly young men without college degrees, this translates into fewer stable job opportunities, reduced wage growth, and diminished prospects for family formation and long-term economic stability.

The cumulative effect is a widening gap between economic classes. While the benefits of low-cost labor are dispersed, often captured by employers and consumers, the costs are concentrated among the most economically vulnerable Americans. Over time, this dynamic reinforces economic immobility, weakens the dignity of work, and contributes to the broader sense that the economic system is no longer structured in the interests of the American worker.

Beyond economics, however, the deeper issue is cultural and civic fragmentation.

In many parts of the country, the rapid scale of illegal immigration has outpaced the nation’s capacity for assimilation. Census data shows that more than one in five people aged 5 and older in the United States now speak a language other than English at home, totaling more than 67 million people, while nearly 8–9 percent of the population, over 25 million people, report speaking English less than “very well.” These figures are significantly higher in major metropolitan areas and certain states.

The effects are especially visible in public education. Nationwide, over 5 million students, more than 10 percent of all public school enrollment, are classified as English Language Learners (ELL), with concentrations exceeding 20 percent in states like California and Texas. In many school districts, this places significant demands on resources and, in many cases, slows instructional pace for entire classrooms.

Beyond schools, the need for multilingual accommodation has become embedded across public institutions. Courts, hospitals, and local governments increasingly rely on translation and interpretation services to function effectively, with federal law reinforcing these requirements. This is no longer a transitional phase of assimilation; it’s become a structural feature of American life. Historically, immigration to the United States was paired with a strong expectation of linguistic assimilation over time. When large populations remain linguistically separate for extended periods, it affects more than communication, it alters the conditions of civic life itself. A shared language is the foundation of democratic participation: it enables citizens to engage with laws, understand public debates, and hold institutions accountable. Without it, civic participation fragments, public discourse becomes siloed, and the sense of a common national life weakens.

The signs of a national collapse are no longer subtle. In major cities and public demonstrations, foreign flags are increasingly displayed with pride on American streets—sometimes not alongside the American flag, but in place of it—signaling a shift in allegiance from assimilation toward persistent identification with countries of origin. At the same time, foreign ownership of American land and property has steadily expanded, with millions of acres of U.S. farmland and strategic real estate now held by foreign nationals and entities, including adversarial nations. This dual phenomenon, cultural detachment at the street level and external acquisition of physical assets at the structural level, reflects that the nation is at risk of not being defined by a unified people with a primary loyalty to their country. The republic cannot endure if large numbers within its borders do not fully identify with it, or if control of its land and resources increasingly shifts beyond its citizens.

Crime and disorder have also emerged as areas of concern, particularly where enforcement of immigration law is weakest. The inability, or unwillingness, of federal authorities to remove every individual who has violated immigration law contributes to a broader perception that laws can be ignored without consequence. That broader perception thus empowers violent offenders, enabling preventable crimes to occur; sometimes with tragic consequences. The murder of Laken Riley, a 22-year-old nursing student killed by an illegal alien, stands as one of the most visible examples of this failure. Similar cases have occurred across the country. In Maryland, Rachel Morin, a mother of five, was raped and murdered. In Texas, 12-year-old Jocelyn Nungaray was killed. And in Chicago, 18-year-old Sheridan Gorman was allegedly murdered by an illegal alien. In each instance the tragedy is not only the crime itself, but the prior breakdown in enforcement that allowed it to happen. When all foreigners who have violated immigration law are not consistently identified, detained, and removed, the government effectively accepts a level of risk that would otherwise be avoidable. This reality contributes to a growing public perception that laws can be ignored without consequence, undermining both deterrence and confidence in the institutions responsible for maintaining public safety.

The consequence of each of these problems is not diversity in the traditional American sense, where newcomers are integrated into a common culture, but parallel societies developing within the same geographic space. Civic participation declines when language barriers persist. Social trust weakens when shared norms become absent. Public life becomes more transactional and less cohesive. Taken together, these realities point to a single conclusion: the American republic cannot survive without mass deportations.

The only solution to this existential crisis for the United States is mass deportation of illegal aliens. If properly carried out, and border and immigration controls are faithfully enforced moving forward, a deportation operation of this scale would not only restore legal order but relieve pressure on public systems, stabilize labor markets for American workers, and reestablish the conditions necessary for cultural assimilation and national cohesion.

President Trump promised not only to secure the border, but to “carry out the largest deportation operation in American history.” During his first year back in office, President Trump, with full resistance from political opponents, special interests, and media, took the first steps to potentially begin such a program. First, and most importantly, he secured a massive influx of resources to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) through a reconciliation package for the purposes of mass deportation. Second, ICE began a very public focus on the arrest and deportation of criminal illegal aliens. As the administration has admitted, the total criminal illegal population is a relatively small subset of the total illegal population—with estimates from members of the Trump Administration ranging from 500,000 to 800,000. At times, this strategy has been referred to as “the worst of the worst” or the “worst first.” This enforcement tactic was not a mass deportation strategy, but one of perceived quality of deportations over quantity. In doing so, ICE resources surged at a small population. The American public witnessed widespread obstruction of ICE, record violence targeting ICE agents, and a complete resistance by some state and local governments. In short, it demonstrated that the political opposition would tolerate no deportations at all.

With little over a year of this administration completed, the time for the first phase of deportations, “the worst first,” should come to an end and advance to phase two: a mass deportation program. The first year can be celebrated as a success for highlighting the quality of the criminal population removed, but the less than 350,000 actual deportations, according to scarce data produced in connection with detention management, don’t represent a victory in quantity. Moreover, recent disclosures that only 72,000 deportable aliens completed their use of the CBP Home app demonstrate that self-deportation is not happening at the rate advertised.

The Trump Administration has at its disposal the resources to execute phase two, even if political opponents refuse to fund the Department of Homeland Security. What remains is a policy choice: to carry out a program of mass deportation, in keeping with the campaign promise, or not. This playbook provides the executive branch policy solutions to keep the promise and achieve at least one million formal deportations in 2026 so that in the years to follow, the numbers can drastically increase in order to provide the long-needed correction to widespread illegal immigration and presence in the United States. With estimates of the total illegal population ranging from the twenty million figure provided by President Trump, and the recent disclosure by Stephen Miller that twenty million illegals came in during the Biden Administration alone, one million deportations in 2026 is a modest start. That modest start can put the operations and policies in place to remove all illegal aliens. This playbook charts the path to do just that.

Notes on Coalition and Playbook

The Mass Deportation Coalition was formed in February 2026 in response to political, operational, legal, and physical attacks on deportation operations. The express purpose of the Mass Deportation Coalition is to support President Trump’s signature campaign promise to “carry out the largest deportation operation in American history.” The Mass Deportation Coalition is composed of immigration law and policy experts, former senior and rank and file law enforcement officials, advocates, and supporters who will provide a permanent support base for mass deportation.

The coalition is united around five key principles that would result in achieving mass deportation and restoring public confidence:

  1. From “Worst-of-the-Worst” to “Phase II: Mass Deportations” — Prioritization of criminal enforcement policy, also known as “worst-of-the-worst,” is rooted in the Clinton Administration and morphed from the exception into the rule during the Obama and Biden Administrations. It is unwarranted in the Trump Administration, as it creates an operational cap on enforcement results. Focusing the bulk of removal resources on a small subset of the removable population results in small removal numbers. Instead, the Phase II focus should be on populations that are easier to remove such as deportable aliens with final orders of removal and visa overstays, and policies like worksite enforcement.
  2. Worksite Enforcement — Worksite enforcement is the most critical missing enforcement policy for the Trump Administration to get on track and meet his agenda. This coalition stands by the key findings of the U.S. Commission on Immigration Reform, led by former Representative Barbara Jordan (D-TX). Too many in Congress have shown disdain for the enforcement of our laws.
  3. Whole of Government Approach — Meaningful numbers of self-deportations will only occur when ICE deportations significantly increase and there is a whole-of-government effort to encourage deportable aliens to leave.
  4. Complete Data Transparency — Regular and complete data transparency from the Trump Administration is a requirement to achieve confidence that the administration is still pursuing his signature campaign promise, which will be his defining policy legacy.
  5. Meaningful Metrics — ICE Interior Removals are defined as a combination of:
    • Expedited Removals from the Interior of the United States;
    • Reinstatement of Removal;
    • Administrative Removals (e.g. aggravated felons); and
    • Removal Orders from an Immigration Judge.
    While the government, over the course of several administrations, has used different components and definitions to arrive at deportation/removal numbers, we will consolidate public understanding of removals as this metric of ICE interior removals. Not included are: turn backs, maritime interdictions, timely self-departures, and untimely self-departures. A subset of untimely self-departures would include CBP Home App completions.

The following playbook represents a menu of policy, operational, and logistical options to achieve at least one million deportations in 2026. The playbook is not intended to be comprehensive. The playbook is a collection of recommendations from participants, and, like any group exercise, is the best summation of consensus as opposed to absolute technical unanimity. It is intended to both prove the feasibility of a mass deportation program and to inspire action. Some of the recommendations are not new types of action, but a scaling of the degree of implementation.

The feasibility of this playbook rests on two pillars: the legal and policy authorities described in the recommendations that follow, and the operational capacity to execute those authorities at scale. The policy recommendations in this document would remain theoretical without a credible operational plan to screen millions of cases, locate and apprehend deportable aliens, detain them securely, and transport them out of the country within the timeframe this campaign demands. That operational plan has been developed by coalition partners with decades of experience in federal law enforcement, military logistics, government contracting, and large-scale transportation operations.

A dramatic shift in strategic philosophy is required to implement this package of recommendations. The Trump Administration must transition the nationwide strategy to include active targeted enforcement of non-criminal deportable aliens, in addition to criminal illegal aliens residing within the United States, leading to their arrest/apprehension and timely deportation. This transition must include an aggressive focus on identifying and, when appropriate, prosecuting U.S. employers who knowingly and willingly hire illegal aliens in violation of the law.

This will require an operational adjustment, including the dedication of enhanced resources and lines of effort targeting the full spectrum of differing categories of deportable aliens, along with political will, to remain steadfast that any deportable alien in the country is a legitimate and necessary target of enforcement and deportation.

The operational environment must open its “prioritization aperture." Resources must be distributed more efficiently and effectively. Supporting entities must be leveraged to effectuate the simultaneous targeting and enforcement of multiple categories of aliens illegally present. Millions of deportable aliens should no longer be treated as a by-product of collateral enforcement by allocating a disproportionate volume of resources towards a small sub-set of criminals.

In short, an effective enforcement strategy must include both a quality and quantity component. These are not mutually exclusive objectives and can be achieved simultaneously. We cannot fall prey to a false binary choice that if we have quantity as an objective, then quality will cease to exist. In fact, the quality of life for Americans will improve in countless ways.

Executive Summary

The following twenty-one recommendations constitute the operational framework of the Mass Deportation Coalition Playbook:

  1. Substantially enhance worksite enforcement
  2. Move the employment verification process online
  3. Debank illegal aliens
  4. Dramatically expand immigration detention
  5. Enforce the alien registration requirements through criminal prosecutions
  6. Deny all visas to nationals of recalcitrant countries
  7. Reform and substantially limit asylum
  8. Enforce civil fines for failure to depart
  9. Expand civil asset forfeiture for immigration violations
  10. Identify and target visa overstays
  11. Download deportation orders and other immigration crime information into NCIC
  12. Transfer authority over no-match letters to the IRS
  13. Leverage Department of Labor authorities
  14. Assign Special Assistant United States Attorneys to prosecute immigration-related crime
  15. Reassign immigration officers within DHS
  16. Place all interior immigration enforcement operations inside the Homeland Security Task Force
  17. Fully utilize other procedures to deport criminal aliens
  18. Litigate challenges vigorously
  19. Leverage States to participate
  20. Track and publicize meaningful benchmarks and statistics
  21. Keep HSI tethered to immigration enforcement
Recommendation 1

Substantially Enhance Worksite Enforcement

There is no chance for a mass deportation program if worksite enforcement is not the centerpiece. Enforcement at scale means focusing on physical areas where illegal aliens are concentrated: worksites. This is how President Eisenhower, who President Trump pledged to surpass in terms of enforcement efforts, was able to achieve his success. The Trump Administration should immediately announce that worksite enforcement will commence at scale. That announcement should be coupled with operational and data transparency as to the dedication of resources to this effort. The administration should track and provide regular statistical accomplishments as they pertain to direct worksite enforcement efforts, such as: the number of worksite investigations; resulting arrests; the number of Blackie’s warrants issued; the number of employer prosecutions; etc.

“Employment continues to be the principal magnet attracting illegal aliens to this country. As long as U.S. businesses benefit from the hiring of unauthorized workers, control of unlawful immigration will be impossible. The Commission believes that both employer sanctions and enhanced labor standards enforcement are essential components of a strategy to reduce the job magnet.” — Barbara Jordan, August 1994 testimony before the Senate Judiciary Committee

Fourteen years later, in 2008, Marcy Forman, director of Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (“ICE”) Office of Investigations, announced an increased focus on criminal enforcement against employers who violate the employer sanctions provisions in section 274A of the INA, explaining:

“The prospect for employment in the United States continues to be one of the leading causes of illegal immigration, creating a market for criminal smuggling organizations who exploit people willing to pay high fees and take great risks to enter the United States without detection.” — Marcy Forman, ICE Office of Investigations, 2008

Although the prospect of employment has long been recognized as the main reason aliens come here illegally, and despite Forman’s claimed focus on employers that hire illegal workers in contravention of section 274A of the INA, worksite enforcement was then and has long been an afterthought in immigration enforcement.

In FY 2007, ICE initiated fewer than 1,100 worksite cases, resulting in 4,077 administrative arrests of illegal alien workers. Seven years later, in FY 2014, worksite cases nearly doubled, but worksite arrests of illegal alien workers declined by 86.7 percent, to just 541.

ICE increased its worksite enforcement efforts during the first Trump Administration, but they resulted in few deportations. In FY 2018, “HSI opened 6,848 worksite investigations compared to 1,691 in FY17,” but agents arrested just 1,525 illegal workers in the course of those investigations.

Congress added the employer sanctions provisions in section 274A to the INA in the same bill that included the “Reagan amnesty,” the Immigration Reform and Control Act of 1986 (IRCA). Ironically, however, in the years after the passage of that bill, arrests of illegal aliens at worksites plummeted. In its 1984 opinion on worksite arrests, Lopez-Mendoza, the Supreme Court explained that “Immigration officers apprehend over one million deportable aliens in this country every year.” The justices also noted that: “In the course of a year, the average INS agent arrests almost 500 illegal aliens.... Most arrests of illegal aliens away from the border occur during farm, factory, or other workplace surveys. Large numbers of illegal aliens are often arrested at one time....”

Today, an estimated 10.8 million to 11.1 million aliens are working here illegally, up from somewhere between 3.5 and six million in the early 1980s. Yet, aside from a few high-profile operations, ICE has not targeted worksites that employ illegal aliens. Consequently, ICE is not arresting and deporting aliens at the levels it did 42 years ago.

The April 2025 Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) between ICE and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) focuses on criminal investigations of aliens who have failed to depart under section 243(a) of the INA. ICE should enter similar agreements with the IRS and other agencies, including and especially the Social Security Administration (SSA), to identify the businesses where aliens are working unlawfully and target them there.

When ICE serves Notices of Suspect Documents in worksite enforcement investigations, it should speak to employees who provided the suspect documents and prepare warrants of arrest under section 236(a) of the INA in advance to take those employees into custody. If business owners refuse agents’ requests to interview their employees or deny them access to their worksites, ICE should apply for and obtain Blackie’s warrants to enter their businesses.

As a former high-ranking INS and ICE official has explained:

“A Blackie’s warrant is a civil search warrant authorizing immigration agents to enter private premises for the purpose of enforcing the civil/administration provisions of law relating to exclusion and deportation. It derives its name from the cases that established their validity—in which a restaurant chain in the metropolitan Washington, D.C., area called Blackie’s House of Beef repeatedly denied entry to immigration agents to search for, and take custody of, illegal aliens in the public and non-public areas of the restaurants.”

Deploying federal resources for worksite enforcement would accomplish multiple goals at the same time. First, since the vast majority of illegal aliens are economic migrants, worksite enforcement would significantly disincentivize the main driver and motivation for illegal immigration into the United States in the first place—economic opportunity for illegal aliens. Fewer illegal aliens will try to come to the United States and those here will be incentivized to leave if their economic opportunities are foreclosed through increased worksite enforcement. Second, if accompanied by a robust employer sanctions program, it would send a message to employers that employ illegal labor that there are real and significant consequences for violating the law and many will stop doing so in order to avoid fines and other penalties. Third, since it is no secret which industries employ large numbers of illegal aliens, worksite enforcement is an operationally low-risk use of resources that would significantly increase the number of interior deportations to accomplish the goal of 1,000,000 deportations in 2026.

Worksite enforcement is only effective to the degree that aliens identified and apprehended at worksites are actually removed from the United States. Historically, worksite operations have produced arrests that were not followed by timely deportation, undermining both deterrence and public confidence. To ensure that worksite enforcement contributes to the mass deportation target, aliens apprehended in worksite operations should be immediately enrolled in the contracted case screening and apprehension pipeline. Cases involving aliens with prior removal orders or clear public charge failures should bypass the litigation phase entirely and proceed to detention and departure. Cases requiring adjudication should be triaged and scheduled on expedited dockets. The operational infrastructure described in this playbook, including the contracted screening teams, deputized apprehension workforce, military installation detention network, and charter air fleet, exists precisely to convert worksite apprehensions into actual removals at the pace and volume this campaign requires. The success of this worksite campaign will largely depend on the aggressive prosecution of the employers of illegal aliens.

Recommendation 2

Move the Employment Verification Process Online

To facilitate employers hiring work-authorized aliens, make the business administration less burdensome for employers, and to more easily identify aliens working without authorization, the Administration should permanently and completely move the Form I-9 employment verification process online.

Section 274A(b) of the INA does not specify how employers must document the identification and work-authorization information they are required to collect, but when that provision was added to the INA in 1986, a paper form was reasonable because technology was limited. Today, however, millions of people file documents with the government online, including multiple tax forms, various federal personnel forms, and most notably, a variety of applications for immigration benefits. Given that, there appear to be few practical impediments that would prevent employers from filing Forms I-9 electronically with DHS. Indeed, in today’s digital world of employment, honest employers would likely prefer it.

In fact, the act itself envisions that the way employers comply with section 274A(b) would change as technology advanced, as illustrated by section 274A(d) of the INA, captioned “Evaluation and changes in employment verification system.” Subparagraph (1)(A) therein directs the President to “provide for the monitoring and evaluation of the degree to which the employment verification system . . . provides a secure system to determine employment eligibility in the United States,” and to “examine the suitability of existing Federal and State identification systems for use for this purpose.”

Given the millions of illegal aliens working in the United States, few would contend the current paper-based Form I-9 verification system in any way “provides a secure system to determine employment eligibility in the United States.” The next subparagraph in the statute, captioned “Improvements to establish secure system,” states:

“To the extent that the system established under subsection (b) is found not to be a secure system to determine employment eligibility in the United States, the President shall, subject to [congressional notification requirements in 274A(d)(3)] and taking into account the results of any demonstration projects conducted under [274A(d)(4)], implement such changes in (including additions to) the requirements of [274A(b)] as may be necessary to establish a secure system to determine employment eligibility in the United States. Such changes in the system may be implemented only if the changes conform to the requirements of [274A(d)(2)].”

The last statutory provision referenced, section 274A(d)(2) of the INA, lists a series of restrictions on proposed changes to what is now the Form I-9 process, most notably on how the information collected is protected and shared across the government, and on new documents the government may require employers to accept. If the Administration does not require employers to seek or accept any new documents, and solely uses the information collected for employment verification purposes under section 274A of the INA and immigration fraud prosecutions, none of those restrictions would appear to bar the implementation of an online Form I-9 filing system.

Key to any changes, therefore, would be the Congressional notification requirements for changes to the current system in section 274A(d)(3), which require the President to notify Congress before making any changes or improvements to the employment verification system. In general, the President must notify the House and Senate Committees on the Judiciary 60 days in advance of making any change, but if that change is a “major change” (as defined in section 274A(d)(3)(D) of the INA), the President must wait one to two years after notifying Congress before making the change.

Only one of the defined “major changes” in section 274A(d)(3)(D) of the INA appears to be even arguably relevant to our proposed Form I-9 online filing system: clause (ii), which describes the following change as “major:”

“a change which would provide for a telephone verification system under which an employer, recruiter, or referrer must transmit to a Federal official information concerning the immigration status of prospective employees and the official transmits to the person, and the person must record, a verification code. . . .”

Moving the I-9 process online would be neither “telephonic” nor need to require the employer to “record a verification code.” Consequently, it would not be a “major change” of the plain language of the statute.

Finally, the retention requirement for employment verification forms in section 274A(b)(3) of the INA would appear to support, if not envision, such a change. It states:

“After completion of such form [the employer] must retain a paper, microfiche, microfilm, or electronic version of the form and make it available for inspection by officers of [DHS], the Special Counsel for Immigration-Related Unfair Employment Practices, or [DOL] during a period beginning on the date of the hiring, recruiting, or referral of the individual and ending – . . . in the case of the hiring of an individual- (i) three years after the date of such hiring, or (ii) one year after the date the individual’s employment is terminated, whichever is later.”

A system that requires employers to file Forms I-9 online directly with DHS would allow ICE to inspect them “at the time of hiring,” and that system could also require employers to maintain an “electronic” version of the form that the Department of Labor (“DOL”) or the Special Counsel could request, which would comply with the rest of the record retention requirement. Accordingly, DHS has clear statutory authority to change the current paper-based Form I-9 employment verification system to an online Form I-9 filing system, provided the President gives Congress 60 days’ notice as required by section 274A(d)(3)(A) before making that change.

This proposal is different from one in which the President could arguably mandate the use of what is known as “E-Verify” by executive action as permitted under section 274A(d) following 60 days’ notice to Congress.

USCIS, which administers E-Verify, explains:

“E-Verify is an Internet-based system that compares information entered by an employer from an employee’s Form I-9, Employment Eligibility Verification, to records available to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and the Social Security Administration to confirm employment eligibility.”

Note that E-Verify notifies employers that specific employees are or do not appear to be employment authorized, whereas moving the Form I-9 filing process online would simply require the employer to forward identification and employment eligibility information to DHS, without any further notification by the government to the employer.

Ideally, the president would mandate E-Verify, which would deny illegal aliens the ability to work without authorization, and thus prompt most to leave voluntarily.

Migrating the current paper-based Form I-9 employment verification process online would provide DHS—and ICE, in particular—ready access to information they need to identify aliens who are working illegally in the United States and facilitate their removal by focusing on the businesses where they are employed.

For each alien who is determined to be working without authorization, ICE should notify several agencies and entities to prevent further downstream economic benefits from unauthorized work. Notified parties should include: USCIS, CBP, the State Department’s Consular Affairs, the employer, IRS, Social Security Administration, banks, lenders, landlords, and relevant state and local agencies to end state government benefits. No remittances from ill-gotten gains of unauthorized work should be permitted. Also, when several employees at one employer are found to be unauthorized to work, public notice should be provided in English that job openings are available to American and lawful immigrant job applicants. It is time to debunk the lies that Americans will not do (an ever-growing list of) jobs. Such public notification of job openings would also refute employers’ false claims that they cannot find American applicants. Of course, this assumes such employers are paying a fair wage, but that issue is beyond the scope of this playbook.

Recommendation 3

Debank Illegal Aliens

Just over six weeks after the September 11th terrorist attacks, Congress passed, and President George W. Bush signed, the Uniting and Strengthening America by Providing Appropriate Tools to Intercept and Obstruct Terrorism Act (PATRIOT Act) of 2001. In part, this law was a response to national-security vulnerabilities identified in the wake of the attacks, including terrorist exploitation of the international banking system, as exemplified by the heading of Title III of the act, the “International Money Laundering Abatement and Anti-Terrorist Financing Act”.

The 9/11 Commission concluded that one impediment that had kept the U.S. government from preventing those attacks was the Treasury Department’s lack of focus on terrorist financing:

“Treasury regulators, as well as U.S. financial institutions, were generally focused on finding and deterring or disrupting the vast flows of U.S. currency generated by drug trafficking and high-level international fraud. Large-scale scandals, such as the use of the Bank of New York by Russian money launderers to move millions of dollars out of Russia, captured the attention of the Department of the Treasury and of Congress. Before 9/11, Treasury did not consider terrorist financing important enough to mention in its national strategy for money laundering.”

Congress, in Title III of the PATRIOT Act, directed the executive branch to close these gaps by refocusing the Treasury Department’s priorities and authorities to disrupt the financing terror organizations relied upon. Section 326 of the PATRIOT Act, “Verification of Identification,” directed the Treasury Secretary to “prescribe regulations setting forth the minimum standards for financial institutions and their customers regarding the identity of the customer that shall apply in connection with the opening of an account at a financial institution.” Congress intended that those regulations would be written to force banks to “implement reasonable procedures for verifying the identity” of their customers.

In May 2003, the Treasury Department, Federal Reserve, Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (“FDIC”), and the National Credit Union Administration (“NCUA”) published their final joint “Know Your Customer” (“KYC”) regulations implementing section 326 of the PATRIOT Act. Specifically, the rule required each bank to implement a “Customer Information Program” (CIP) by October 1, 2003, but the regulations distinguished between a given customer who is a “U.S. person,” i.e., a U.S. citizen or “an individual (such as a corporation, partnership, or trust), that is established or organized under the laws of a State or the United States,” and one who is a “non-U.S. person,” defined simply as “a person that is not a U.S. person.”

Those regulations mandated that each CIP “contain procedures for opening an account that specify the identifying information that will be obtained from each customer,” including the customer’s (1) name; (2) date of birth; (3) address; and (4) an “identification number.” For a U.S. person, that identification number could be a Social Security number, individual taxpayer identification number (ITIN), or employer identification number (EIN), collectively referred to as a “taxpayer identification number.”

A non-U.S. person, however, could present one or more of the following numbers to satisfy the regulatory CIP requirement: “a taxpayer identification number; passport number and country of issuance; alien identification card number; or number and country of issuance of any other government-issued document evidencing nationality or residence and bearing a photograph or similar safeguard.” In other words, and notwithstanding Congress’s intent in section 326 of the PATRIOT Act, the regulation implementing it permits aliens to present a wider range of less-readily identifiable, more-easily counterfeited, and less secure documents for CIP purposes than U.S. citizens can. As the rule explained in a footnote, the regulation “provides this flexibility” to aliens “because there is no uniform identification number that non-U.S. persons would be able to provide to a bank.”

Worse, the rule conceded that:

“Treasury and the Agencies recognize that there currently is no method that would permit a bank to verify, for example, a taxpayer identification, passport or alien identification number through an official source.... Thus, a bank need not establish the accuracy of every element of identifying information obtained but must do so for enough information to form a reasonable belief it knows the true identity of the customer.”

As George Fishman, a former senior congressional staffer who assisted in the drafting of the PATRIOT Act observed last August, “the regulations that the Treasury Department actually wrote turned Congress’s intent” in the act “on its head.” Fishman continued:

“Especially when the Trump administration is rightfully encouraging illegal aliens to ‘self-deport’, it makes absolutely no sense to keep Treasury Department regulations on the books that purposefully make it easier for illegal aliens to remain in the U.S. The misbegotten regulations, which should never have been promulgated in the first place, need to be repealed.”

Recent reports suggest the Trump Administration is considering an executive action to “require banks to collect citizenship information from customers” and “ultimately task banks with asking for an unprecedented new category of documents, such as passports, from both new and existing customers who want to maintain a bank account in the U.S.”

Glaring national security vulnerabilities aside, the current CIP regulations facilitate the continued presence of illegal aliens in the United States. If jobs are the “magnet” that draws aliens illegally to the United States, access to the U.S. banking system is one factor that allows them to remain here, as it enables them to shelter their wages in our secure financial system and to send remittances abroad.

Consequently, and to effectuate the clear intent of Congress in section 326 of the PATRIOT Act, the Treasury Department should revise its “Know Your Customer” and “Customer Identification Program” regulations to bar aliens who cannot establish they are lawfully present in the United States from opening or maintaining bank accounts in the United States.

Similarly, DOJ and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (“CFPB”) published a “joint statement” in the Federal Register under the Biden Administration in October 2023 that purported “to assist creditors and borrowers in understanding the potential civil rights implications of a creditor’s consideration of an individual’s immigration status under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act (‘ECOA’).” The ECOA “prohibits creditors from discriminating against credit applicants” based on “race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age, because an applicant receives income from a public assistance program, or because an applicant has in good faith exercised any right under the Consumer Credit Protection Act.”

That vaguely worded 2023 statement appears to threaten lenders with prosecution under U.S. civil rights laws if they considered an alien’s illegal status in the United States in withholding credit. Specifically, it stated:

“ECOA does not expressly prohibit consideration of immigration status, and, as explained further below, a creditor may consider an applicant’s immigration status when necessary to ascertain the creditor’s rights regarding repayment. However, creditors should be aware that unnecessary or overbroad reliance on immigration status in the credit decisioning process, including when that reliance is based on bias, may run afoul of ECOA’s antidiscrimination provisions, and could also violate other laws.”

If aliens are present illegally, they are not authorized to work and are subject to deportation, two factors directly relevant to the likelihood they will be able to repay their loans. What “overbroad reliance in immigration status” means in the credit process is open to debate, but no lender should be deterred in any way from denying credit to an alien here illegally. It is unclear whether CFPB and DOJ have revised or rescinded their Biden-era “guidance,” but both agencies should revisit their October 2023 statement to make clear that not only is it acceptable for lenders to deny credit to illegal aliens, but it is also appropriate for them to do so.

Recommendation 4

Dramatically Expand Immigration Detention

Detention is mandatory for many classes of removable aliens. For decades, however, ICE has failed to comply with Congress’s detention mandates, and in many previous administrations simply ignored them. ICE should have sufficient bed space to detain every single immigration lawbreaker whose detention is mandatory under the provisions of the Immigration and Nationality Act, along with a surplus to respond to immigration emergencies such as the Mariel Boat Lift.

DHS received $45 billion “for single adult alien detention capacity and family residential center capacity” in H.R. 1, the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” (OBBBA), after decades of being denied adequate detention resources by Congress. We applaud the administration’s efforts to use that funding to expand DHS detention facilities and to enter into contracts with private detention operators and state and local prisons and jails. It is critical to increase the number of “daily beds” available to house aliens while they are in removal proceedings and under final removal orders. Mandatory detention is also required for asylum applicants who illegally crossed the border illegally or without a valid visa. DHS must continue to prioritize the expansion of detention capacity.

The Fifth Circuit recently cited a 1997 report in which the DOJ Inspector General (DOJ IG) concluded that “when aliens are released from custody, nearly 90 percent abscond and are not removed from the United States.” The nearly 75,000 in absentia orders issued by IJs in just the first three months of FY 2026 alone suggests that trend has only gotten worse in the intervening 28 years.

Increased detention capacity would serve other purposes, aside from complying with the INA and ensuring aliens appear for immigration court hearings and for removal. Detained removal cases move much more quickly than hearings in the non-detained setting. The median completion time for a detained immigration court case was 40 days in FY 2018, an increase from the eight days it took to complete the median detained case in FY 2008. Even under the Biden Administration in FY 2023, the median pending time for a detained case was 52 days, compared to an average wait time of 1.7 years (in general) to 4.3 years (in cases where the alien has made an asylum claim) for non-detained immigration court proceedings. Faster adjudications in detention mean respondents who merit relief or protection receive it more quickly, enabling ICE to deport more aliens here unlawfully, while removing incentives for other aliens to delay their removal orders by filing weak or bogus asylum claims. In addition, if aliens with final removal orders are in ICE custody, they cannot abscond and are more likely to cooperate with the agency in obtaining travel documents, thus speeding deportations.

To meet the detention capacity required by a mass deportation campaign, DHS should direct the construction of temporary detention and out-processing facilities on federal military installations nationwide. Military bases offer four critical advantages that no commercial or state-contracted facility can replicate at scale.

First, controlled perimeters. Military installations have existing security infrastructure, including fenced boundaries, gate access controls, and military police presence, eliminating the need to build standalone security systems for each new detention site.

Second, airfield access. Many major military installations include runways and aerial ports of embarkation capable of receiving charter aircraft. Co-locating detention facilities with departure airfields eliminates the logistical burden and security risk of transporting deportees across public roads and through commercial airports. The existing military power projection infrastructure, including installations such as Fort Cavazos (TX), Fort Liberty (NC), Fort Bliss (TX), Fort Campbell (KY), Fort Stewart (GA), Joint Base Lewis-McChord (WA), and Camp Pendleton (CA), among others, already pairs ground facilities with designated aerial ports of embarkation. These installations should serve as the backbone of the detention-to-departure logistics network.

Third, federal jurisdiction conveys legal advantages.

Fourth, speed of construction. Temporary, self-contained facilities, including modular housing, messing, medical services, power generation, water, and sewage, can be erected on military installations in under a week depending on scale. These facilities require no connection to local utility infrastructure and impose no burden on base resources.

The private sector has demonstrated the capacity to erect and operate such facilities at scale, including camps capable of housing over 15,000 individuals, for both military and civilian government clients. DHS should leverage this existing commercial capability through contracted construction and facility management. In addition to newly constructed facilities, DHS should convert existing border processing centers into out-processing and departure facilities. The approximately 190 processing centers currently operating along the southern border and at major airports were designed to intake arriving aliens; reversing the flow to process departing deportees requires minimal infrastructure modification. These facilities should be supplemented, not replaced, by the military installation network.

The combination of military installation detention, border out-processing centers, and expanded use of state and local jails under IGA and 287(g) agreements creates a tiered detention network capable of supporting one million removals in 2026. Bed space, however, is only useful if the logistics of departure keep pace with the rate of apprehension. Detention without timely deportation merely converts an enforcement success into a resource drain. The transportation infrastructure described below is therefore inseparable from the detention expansion.

Recommendation 5

Enforce Alien Registration Requirements Through Criminal Prosecutions

The final report of the 9/11 Commission underscored the importance of identifying aliens in the United States, and yet for decades the INS and then DHS never used the registration tools in Section 262 of the INA to keep track of them. That has changed under the second Trump Administration. It is now incumbent on USCIS and ICE to begin enforcing the penalties in sections 264, 265, and 266 of the INA to ensure every alien in the United States registers with the government.

The information those aliens provide in the registration process will enable ICE to identify aliens here illegally and determine where those aliens reside. The agency should use that information to place those aliens into removal proceedings and, as appropriate, arrest and deport them. Plainly, many if not most of those aliens would prefer to remain “in the shadows,” but to ensure compliance with the new registration rules, the agency should prosecute under section 266 of the INA every alien it encounters who has failed to register, to make clear to all here unlawfully that they will face consequences for violating the law.

Given the choice between registration—essentially notifying DHS of their presence in the United States and providing their addresses—and voluntary departure from this country, many aliens will choose the latter. Self-deportation will preserve scarce department resources while helping to restore credibility to our immigration system. The punishment for willful non-registration—up to 6 months’ confinement and/or up to a $1,000 fine—is not harsh, but the threat of such punishment should be sufficient to ensure compliance or self-deportation.

The Selective Service

With few exceptions, all males between the ages of 18 and 26 living in the United States are required by law to register for the Selective Service. This registration requirement also applies to illegal aliens. Failure to register is a criminal offense. A conviction for violating the Military Service Act can result in imprisonment for up to five years and/or a fine up to $250,000. The Immigration and Nationality Act makes a conviction for failing to register for the Selective Service a deportable offense.

The Selective Service’s website makes it clear that illegal aliens are required to register for the draft, but they also note that they collect no data on the number of illegal aliens who have complied with their legal obligation to register. Records obtained under the Freedom of Information Act reveal that the Selective Service has no data on the number of illegal aliens that have registered or failed to register for the draft.

Obtaining clarity on the number of illegal aliens that have failed to register for the Selective Service and subsequent prosecutions by the Department of Justice for failure to register would increase the number of deportable aliens and subsequent removals.

No foreign national has a right to enter and reside in the United States in contravention of our laws, but if they are here, the American people have a right to know who and where they are to better assess any risks they may pose and determine what costs they may impose on the public fisc.

Recommendation 6

Deny All Visas to Nationals of Recalcitrant Countries

Recalcitrant countries are those countries that refuse to provide travel documents to their nationals who are being removed from the United States. This is a significant impediment to deportation. Congress, however, provided a solution in section 243(d) of the INA. That provision states:

“On being notified by the Attorney General that the government of a foreign country denies or unreasonably delays accepting an alien who is a citizen, subject, national, or resident of that country after the Attorney General asks whether the government will accept the alien under this section, the Secretary of State shall order consular officers in that foreign country to discontinue granting immigrant visas or nonimmigrant visas, or both, to citizens, subjects, nationals, and residents of that country until the Attorney General notifies the Secretary that the country has accepted the alien.”

That authority was used in the first Trump Administration, and in section 13 of his January 20, 2025, EO 14,159, “Protecting the American People Against Invasion,” the returning President directed the Secretary of Homeland Security to:

“Cooperate and effectively implement, as appropriate, the sanctions provided by section 243(d) of the INA…with the Secretary of State, to the maximum extent permitted by law, ensuring that diplomatic efforts and negotiations with foreign states include the foreign states’ acceptance of their nationals who are subject to removal from the United States; and (b) Eliminate all documentary barriers, dilatory tactics, or other restrictions that prevent the prompt repatriation of aliens to any foreign state.”

Days later, Secretary of State Marco Rubio briefly suspended visa issuance at the U.S. Embassy in Colombia after the country’s president refused to accept two repatriation flights to which he had previously agreed. On April 5, 2025, Rubio used his 243(d) authority to revoke visas issued to nationals of South Sudan, and to bar future visa issuances to South Sudanese.

To date, however, DOS has not used its section 243(d) authority as vigorously as it should, even though in July 2025, the Federation for American Immigration Reform (FAIR) reported:

Fully uncooperative countries (15): Bhutan, Burma, Cuba, Congo (DRC), Eritrea, Ethiopia, Hong Kong, India, Iran, Laos, Pakistan, China, Russia, Somalia, and Venezuela.
Countries at risk of non-compliance (11): Bosnia-Herzegovina, Burkina Faso, Cambodia, Gabon, Gambia, Iraq, Jamaica, Nicaragua, South Sudan, St. Lucia, and Vietnam.

To ensure all aliens under final removal orders can be deported, DHS should provide the State Department with a list of foreign nationals for whom it is unable to secure travel documents, and DOS should immediately halt all visa processing in those recalcitrant nations until they provide ICE with needed travel documents and accept the return of their nationals.

Likewise, USCIS should not adjudicate benefit applications from foreign nationals of those recalcitrant countries; ICE should scrutinize SEVIS (Student and Exchange Visitor Information System) for immigration enforcement against student and exchange visitors violating the terms of their visas; and CBP should identify visa overstayers from such countries for removal, based on their Entry/Exit matching.

Recommendation 7

Reform and Substantially Limit Asylum

Before DHS can deport most aliens, it must first obtain final removal orders from the immigration court or the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA). More than 63 percent of the nearly 3.8 million cases in the immigration court backlog involve asylum applications. Consequently, the success of any deportation program depends on expediting decisions on those applications.

Over 63% of the nearly 3.8 million cases in the immigration court backlog involve asylum applications. Section 208(d)(5)(A)(iii) mandates final adjudication within 180 days.

For years, Senator Ron Johnson (R-WI) has published and updated a version of the chart above detailing monthly Southwest Border encounters since 2012. While the chart includes the implementation dates of key policies across administrations and the corresponding rise or fall in illegal migration, the main legal vehicle by which the majority of illegal aliens remain in the United States during the pendency of their immigration proceedings is by claiming asylum.

Section 208(d)(5)(A)(iii) of the INA mandates that “in the absence of exceptional circumstances, final administrative adjudication of the asylum application, not including administrative appeal, shall be completed within 180 days after the date an application is filed.” Few if any Immigration Judge (IJ) adjudications, outside of detention, comply with that standard.

Moreover, the asylum standards are stringent, limiting protection to aliens who can show first, that they suffered past persecution or have a “well-founded fear of” future persecution and second, that the alien’s race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group was or will be “at least a central factor” for such persecution. Poverty, war, crime, deprivation and even direct threats abroad do not by themselves satisfy that standard.

There are four reasons why the immigration courts struggle to complete asylum cases in a timely and appropriate manner.

1. Fraud

Under the asylum statute, applicants’ own testimony “may be sufficient to sustain” their burden to show eligibility “without corroboration,” under a reasonable principle that “persecutors don’t provide affidavits.” The executive branch has tools to uncover and root out that fraud, but their use requires both focus and resources.

The State Department operates globally, including in most countries from which aliens seek asylum. By regulation, IJs may ask DOS to comment on any pending asylum application. The process for requesting comments, however, is not standardized, but that is an issue that EOIR and DOS could—and should—easily resolve.

Moreover, there is currently no method to forensically investigate a claim made by an alien who has been granted asylum, even though asylum grants place aliens on a path to citizenship. ICE ERO (Enforcement and Removal Operations) and HSI, DOS Consular Affairs (CA) and Bureau of Diplomatic Security (DS), and/or USCIS FDNS could, however, be tasked with choosing a representative sample of approved asylum claims and performing foreign in-country investigations of those claims. If fraud is uncovered during those investigations, applicants should be prosecuted under 18 U.S.C. § 1546, a crime that carries a sentence of up to 10 to 25 years of imprisonment. In any event, such investigations would also assist in identifying other fraudulent asylum claims.

FDNS began such an investigation in the early 2000s as part of its Benefit Fraud Assessment (BFA) Program. Louis Crocetti, former FDNS director, described the results to the House Immigration Subcommittee in 2014. According to Crocetti, out of 239 cases FDNS randomly selected that were pending with or completed by USCIS between May 1 and October 31, 2005:

30 percent (72 cases) did not have any “fraud indicators;”
12 percent (29 cases) were “determined to be fraudulent;” and
58 percent (138 cases) “exhibited possible indicators of fraud.”

Fifty-nine of the 138 cases with indicia of fraud were sent overseas for verification by USCIS or DOS, and of the 26 cases in which overseas investigations were completed, 17 (65 percent) “resulted in a finding of fraud.” Unfortunately, the FDNS BFA asylum investigation was never finalized, but it reveals how prevalent fraud is in the asylum process and also provides a template for future investigations.

Now, AI tools should be applied to applications to more quickly and easily identify fraud, deny such applications, and remove the applicants because fraud makes them ineligible for all forms of immigration benefits.

2. Volume

The second reason why immigration courts struggle to adjudicate asylum applications in a timely manner has to do with volume. Any alien facing removal can apply for asylum, with specific exceptions discussed below, and consequently most do. As the Supreme Court has recognized, “every delay works to the advantage of the deportable alien who wishes merely to remain in the United States.” As aliens with pending asylum applications cannot be removed, it is an ideal stall tactic for aliens with much to gain and little to lose. Those incentives have long caused immigration court and BIA dockets to swell.

Nor are there many current deterrents to dissuade aliens from filing weak, non-existent, or bogus asylum claims simply to delay removal. Section 208(d)(6) of the INA provides that if IJs, the BIA, or USCIS “determines that an alien has knowingly made a frivolous application for asylum…the alien shall be permanently ineligible for any” immigration benefits. The problem is that the regulation implementing that bar states that applications filed prior to January 11, 2021, are only considered “frivolous” if:

“Any of the material elements in the asylum application is deliberately fabricated, and the immigration judge or the Board is satisfied that the applicant, during the course of the proceedings, has had sufficient opportunity to account for any discrepancies or implausible aspects of the claim.”

Given the size of the immigration court backlog, there are likely tens to hundreds of thousands of pending cases that were filed prior to January 2021, but that definition is a more apt description of “fraud” than “frivolousness.” It is unlikely to deter any alien who filed before that date from proceeding with their weak or legally deficient claim.

Additionally, note that the January 2021 date was established as a response to comments filed opposing the proposed version of this rule. Those comments argued that without establishing the prospective January 2021 onset date when the rule was finalized in 2020, the rule would be subject to invalidation as retroactive. The agencies (DOJ and DHS) noted that most of what they had proposed to do in the rule as to frivolous asylum claims were mere clarifications of law, relying on Levy v. Sterling Holding Company, and thus that they had not proposed rules that would have impermissible retroactive effect. The agencies were nevertheless persuaded to make their clarifications carry only prospective effect. Nothing forecloses the agencies from promulgating a new final rule accepting the risk of a retroactivity-based injunction or vacatur, in order to try to achieve the upside of weeding out thousands of frivolous asylum applications. In short, asylum claims filed before January 2021 should not be regarded as somehow sacrosanct. A new, less risk-averse rule could make substantial inroads in solving the problem of the backlog.

As for an asylum application filed after that date, it would be considered frivolous if it:

  • (1) Contains a fabricated material element;
  • (2) Is premised upon false or fabricated evidence unless the application would have been granted without the false or fabricated evidence;
  • (3) Is filed without regard to the merits of the claim; or
  • (4) Is clearly foreclosed by applicable law.

That definition is more in line with Congress’s intent, but IJs are often reluctant to make findings that even the most legally deficient asylum applications are frivolous. The Attorney General or BIA could rectify that by issuing a precedent opinion that clearly delineates when a legally invalid asylum application must be considered “frivolous” and that highlights the deleterious impact deficient claims are imposing on the overall backlog and on the courts’ inability to comply with the 180-day deadline in section 208(d)(5)(A)(iii) of the INA.

3. Work Authorization Incentivizes Filing

Third, and relatedly, the ready availability of work authorization incentivizes aliens to file asylum applications, even if their claims are weak, deficient, non-existent, or fraudulent. Under current regulations, an alien can receive work authorization 180 days after filing an asylum application, if that application has not been adjudicated and denied. The Trump Administration has proposed a rule to extend that 180-day deadline to 365 days, and to pause receipts of applications when the average processing times for asylum applications exceed 180 days. That rule would be a positive step but the administration should go further and revoke work authorization for any alien who concedes removability, and only reinstate it if and when the alien is ultimately granted asylum.

4. Related Protections

A fourth reason why asylum applications are clogging the immigration courts has to do with the related humanitarian protections of statutory withholding of removal (“statutory withholding”) and the Convention Against Torture (CAT). Numerous exceptions in section 208(a)(2) of the INA bar aliens from applying for asylum, most notably a requirement that aliens must seek that protection within one year of arrival (the “one-year bar”). An “asylum application,” Form I-589, is also an application for statutory withholding and CAT, however, and the one-year bar does not apply to those protections. Accordingly, an alien could enter illegally, reside here for a decade, and be allowed to apply for statutory withholding and CAT only after being encountered by DHS and placed into removal proceedings.

Further, there are additional exceptions that prevent IJs and USCIS from granting asylum to certain categories of aliens—including (1) persecutors, aliens convicted of aggravated felonies and other “particularly serious crimes,” (2) aliens who “committed a serious nonpolitical crime outside the United States,” and (3) aliens who pose a danger to national security. To be clear, those aliens can still file I-589s with the immigration court seeking asylum, and IJs must still go through the process of considering their applications to determine whether those bars apply and to adjudicate their statutory withholding and CAT claims.

Many of those same bars to asylum—for persecutors, those who have “committed a serious nonpolitical crime outside the United States,” and aliens who pose a danger to national security—also preclude the immigration court from granting statutory withholding. That said, only aliens who have been convicted of an aggravated felony and “sentenced to an aggregate term of imprisonment of at least 5 years” are dispositively barred from statutory withholding, though IJs can find that crimes that are not aggravated felonies or are aggravated felonies for which the alien received a sentence of less than 5 years are “particularly serious” for purposes of that bar. Again, that is a resource-intensive process that slows IJ adjudications.

Finally, nothing bars any alien from being granted deferral of removal under CAT, meaning even the most egregious criminals and dangerous terrorists can delay removal by seeking that protection. Osama bin-Laden, had he lived, could have sought CAT deferral and an IJ would have been required to consider his claim. Note, however, that CAT protection does not arise from any provision of the INA but instead is a function of the U.N. Convention Against Torture, which the United States signed in October 1994.

As the Congressional Research Service has explained: “The United States ratified CAT subject to certain declarations, reservations, and understandings, including that the Convention was not self-executing, and therefore required domestic implementing legislation to take effect.” Congress implemented CAT in section 2242 of the Foreign Affairs Reform and Restructuring Act of 1998 (FARRA), which made it U.S. policy “not to expel, extradite, or otherwise effect the involuntary removal of any person to a country where there are substantial grounds for believing that the person would be in danger of being subjected to torture.” FARRA did not expressly explain how that policy was to be applied, however, leaving it to the “appropriate” executive-branch agencies to enact regulations to enforce those CAT protections.

Note also that IJs and the BIA did not originally have jurisdiction over CAT claims from aliens facing removal. From the date CAT was ratified in November 1994 until the issuance of a rule implementing FARRA (effective March 22, 1999), the then-INS adopted its own administrative process to determine whether CAT protection should be extended in “individual cases in which an alien is subject to removal.”

As the implementing rule explained:

“Under this pre-regulatory administrative process, upon completion of deportation, exclusion, or removal proceedings and prior to execution of a final order of removal, the INS has considered whether removing an alien to a particular country is consistent with [CAT]. If it is determined that the alien could not be removed to the country in question consistent with [CAT], the INS has used its existing discretionary authority to ensure the alien is not removed to that country for so long as he or she is likely to be tortured there.”
“This approach has allowed the INS to address the applicability of Article 3 to a case only when actually necessary to comply with the Convention. It has also allowed an individual alien to exhaust all avenues for pursuing any other more extensive benefit or protection for which he or she may be eligible before seeking the minimal guarantee provided by Article 3 that he or she will not be returned to a specific country where it is likely that he or she would be tortured.”
“At the same time, this approach has allowed the INS, the agency responsible for executing removal orders, to ensure that no order is executed under circumstances that would violate [CAT].”

If that pre-regulatory process, under which the then-INS (not IJs or the BIA) adjudicated CAT requests, was sufficient “to ensure that no” deportation order was “executed under circumstances that would violate” the convention, there is no reason to believe INS’s successor agencies in DHS would not be able to do the same. Shifting CAT determinations from the immigration courts to DHS would free IJs from having to adjudicate CAT applications, particularly those filed by aliens who are not statutorily eligible for any other immigration relief.

To reduce the immigration court backlog and expedite deportations, DOJ and DHS should revisit their 1999 CAT regulation and give ICE ERO officers or USCIS asylum officers sole authority to adjudicate torture claims made by aliens. More generally, the administration should republish its June 2020, “global asylum rule,” which would have made additional crucial reforms to the asylum system but was enjoined weeks before the end of the first Trump Administration by the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California. That rule has never been fully litigated, but the President’s remaining term would provide the DOJ sufficient time to defend it.

In addition, both relief under CAT and asylum can be terminated for changed circumstances and other reasons. ICE should reexamine CAT and asylum grants for select countries in which circumstances have changed, and such relief is no longer warranted. ICE should likewise apply AI tools to granted asylum cases, including aliens who subsequently obtained a green card and naturalization, to search for asylum fraud indicated by aliens who travelled to their home country after claiming fear of returning there.

Finally, over 300,000 removal cases are currently administratively closed in the immigration court system. In effect, the cases of these removable aliens have been shelved, and the alien continues living and likely working in the U.S., which is why the Trump Administration has since labeled these cases “amnesty cases.” A sizable portion of administratively closed cases are aliens who were granted Temporary Protected Status (TPS) by USCIS. The Administration has terminated TPS designations for several countries, however. As such, these and other administratively closed cases should be re-opened and brought to conclusion. Deportable aliens should not be given an administrative amnesty to prolong their stay indefinitely in the U.S. to wait for some speculative future immigration benefit.

In addition, the Biden Administration terminated or dismissed another 855,000 cases because they were non-priority cases or for lagging paperwork. These aliens have also been given administrative amnesty. Because these aliens are removable, ICE should place them in removal proceedings again, with all applicable charges, and pursue the cases to their end.

Recommendation 8

Enforce Civil Fines for Failure to Depart

In addition to the criminal sanctions in section 243(a)(1) for aliens who fail to depart within 90 days, section 274D of the INA mandates civil fines for aliens who:

  • Willfully fail or refuse to depart the United States pursuant to a final removal order;
  • Willfully fail or refuse to “make timely application in good faith for travel or other documents necessary for departure”; or
  • Fail to appear for removal in response to a bag and baggage letter.
Those fines are now set at $998 per day.

At a minimum, the department (in conjunction with DOJ) should impose those fines and place liens on the real and personal property of aliens who remain in the United States in contravention of the departure requirements in the INA.

Recommendation 9

Expand Civil Asset Forfeiture for Immigration Violations

ICE has explained that “[s]eizures and forfeitures are some of the most powerful tools” in its arsenal: “Asset forfeiture financially hurts the violator. Over the years, the emphasis has been shifting from merely putting the violator in jail to putting the violator in jail with no assets.”

Civil Asset Forfeiture (CAF) is an appropriate and viable tool to support immigration enforcement. Many actions that facilitate illegal migration to, and residence in, the United States—the use of fraudulent documents, identity theft, false statements, fee-based smuggling deals, and the movement of illicit proceeds through remittances—already involves financial gain derived from statutory violations.

In this context, CAF would allow ICE to target the economic incentives that sustain unlawful presence and unauthorized employment, and to seize assets traceable to fraud-derived wages or other immigration-related offenses. Applied with clear thresholds and supervisory review, CAF can serve as a powerful deterrent to future illegal immigration by reducing financial payoffs related to unauthorized employment and increasing the risk that fraud-derived assets will be seized.

For aliens here illegally, the prospect of losing vehicles, bank accounts, tools, or money for remittances would encourage voluntary departure long before removal proceedings conclude or likely even begin. For employers, and in particular repeat violators who knowingly accept fraudulent documents, pay off the books, or profit from illegal labor, the possibility of forfeiture provides a meaningful consequence in a legal environment where criminal sanctions are difficult to prove and civil penalties are rarely imposed.

Used judiciously and with clear internal guardrails, CAF could disrupt or dismantle the financial infrastructure of immigration violations without relying solely on detention or removal. CAF would not replace employer sanctions, but could supplement worksite enforcement. It would fill the accountability gap and target the economic incentives that drive both unauthorized employment and the businesses that depend on it, promoting compliance through the credible threat of financial loss rather than costly mass prosecution.

Recommendation 10

Identify and Target Visa Overstays

Prior to the Biden Administration and its open-borders policies, which facilitated the illegal entry and unlawful presence of millions of illegal migrants, it was estimated that 42 percent of the illegal population in the United States, and 66 percent of new additions to that population, were aliens who had been admitted as nonimmigrants but violated their statuses or failed to depart as required. The annual number of such “overstays” has likely not declined in the interim, and with the Southwest border now operationally secure, those aliens represent the largest additions to the illegal population.

Before nonimmigrant visa violators and overstays can be targeted for enforcement, however, DHS must first identify and find them. The DHS secretary should task CBP officers in OFO (Office of Field Operations) to cull nonimmigrant departure records on an ongoing basis to identify suspected nonimmigrant overstays (including those admitted on Border Crossing Cards) and send that information to ICE ERO monthly, for investigation and removal purposes.

To identify visa overstayers, we applaud the Administration for publishing a 2025 final rule to complete the biometric Entry-Exit system that Congress first required 30 years ago. Although Land Exit for vehicles has been the missing segment for completing implementation, we believe this Administration already created at least part of the solution when CBP designed the CBP Home application for self-deportations. By attaching a photo and GPS location, CBP can use facial matching technology to verify the correct person has indeed departed the U.S.
