CBP should go further by requiring all visa holders to download an app such as CBP Home, on which CBP enters a visa holder’s “Admit Until” date to remind the alien by when the alien must depart the U.S. CBP should then push notifications to the alien as the departure deadline approaches, indicating it is time for the visa holder to make departure travel arrangements and warn that failure to depart by the date or show proof of a change of immigration status will turn into a violation of the law and the alien will be subject to deportation. To demonstrate real consequences, ICE should publicize that a significant number of visa overstayers are being deported. This combination of regular CBP communication with visa holders and the imposition of visible consequences for failing to timely depart will change behavior and thus should increase visa compliance and timely departures.

Recommendation 11

Download Deportation Orders and Other Immigration Crime Information into NCIC

The National Crime Information Center (NCIC), one of a group of national crime information systems managed by the Criminal Justice Information Services Division (CJIS) at the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), is “used by the public safety community for both criminal and civil purposes.” CJIS describes NCIC as a “criminal records database allowing criminal justice agencies to enter or search for information about stolen property, missing or wanted persons, and domestic violence protection orders; to get criminal histories; and to access the National Sex Offender Registry.”

NCIC has traditionally included immigration-enforcement information related to orders of removal and deportation and failures to appear for removal. These notifications can alert local law enforcement officers about a suspect’s immigration history and DHS’s interest in the alien. An alien’s status can change after an order of removal is issued, however. For example, the alien’s case may be reopened, or the alien may qualify for Temporary Protected Status, either of which would preclude removal. This has made NCIC less effective in the immigration context than it could be.

With the additional resources provided by the OBBBA, ICE should:

  • Update the immigration violations it submits to NCIC;
  • Exclude aliens who are no longer removable;
  • Add information related to the hundreds of thousands of aliens who have recently been removed; and
  • Submit information to NCIC on aliens who potentially could be prosecuted for immigration-related offenses, including eluding inspection under section 275(a)(2) of the INA, failure to register and to update addresses in violation of section 266(a) and (b) (respectively), and failure to depart under section 275(a).

Even in “sanctuary” jurisdictions, many, if not most, police officers have an interest in assisting other law enforcement agencies, including ICE. Many are prohibited from doing so, however, under local policies. A “want” in NCIC for an alien who faces possible criminal punishment for an immigration-related crime may eliminate such impediments, which generally only restrict and prohibit state and local assistance in “civil” immigration enforcement.

In states and localities that are more supportive of ICE enforcement, up-to-date and reliable immigration information in NCIC would enable local authorities to better assist DHS in identifying, arresting, detaining, and deporting aliens sought by the department.

Recommendation 12

Transfer Authority Over No-Match Letters to the IRS

Over the past couple of decades, the Social Security Administration (SSA) has periodically sent letters to employers to notify them of employees whose Social Security numbers (SSNs) do not match the names associated with those numbers in SSA’s database. The goal of these letters is to let employers know that the listed employees may be illegal aliens using fake or stolen SSNs for employment purposes.

This policy should be uncontroversial since it is illegal for employers to hire aliens without work authorization, illegal for individuals to use fraudulent or stolen SSNs, and harmful to the rightful owner of an SSN whose number has been stolen by an illegal alien. Two problems arise with these “No-Match” letters, however:

  • The letters generally do not give the employers specific instructions on how to resolve the no-match; and
  • SSA has no real way to apply consequences to employers that fail to take action.

One solution to these problems is to transfer the authority to send the No-Match letters to the Internal Revenue Service (IRS). The IRS already has access to the names, SSNs, and employers of all employees through payroll taxes, so no new information would need to be shared between federal agencies, though SSA would need to cooperate with the IRS to confirm the no-matches.

The IRS should send the No-Match letters on a semi-annual basis (either quarterly or biannually) to all employers of individuals whose name does not match the SSN they provided. These letters should instruct the employers that they must take specific steps to verify that the employees are, in fact, legally authorized to work in the United States, and require them to provide a valid, matching SSN. If the employee cannot do so, the employer should be instructed to terminate the employee within 90 days and tell him or her to register with the CBP-Home app, so as to collect a plane ticket and cash upon departure from the country.

Giving the employer 90 days to terminate the employee would provide ample time for the employer to find a legal replacement for the employee and thus cause minimal disruption at the worksite.

Finally, the No-Match letter should apprise the employer of the potential consequences of failure to verify the employee’s work authorization and provide a valid SSN or, alternatively, to terminate employment. An employer that has not terminated an unverified employee, based on payroll tax data, should be subject to:

  • An audit by the IRS to determine the total amount of wages deducted by the employer that were paid to unverified employees over the past seven years. These would be unlawful deductions, since it is illegal to employ aliens without work authorization, subject to back taxes and interest penalties; and
  • Enforcement action by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). The IRS should notify ICE of each instance where an employer failed to comply with the requirements laid out in the No-Match letter.

Employers may be inclined to disregard letters from SSA, but they are much less likely to disregard letters, with clear instructions, from the IRS. Especially when there are potentially severe consequences. Transferring authority for No-Match letters to the IRS, and enforcing them, would be a significant step toward making illegal aliens unemployable in the United States.

Similar to the unauthorized employment notifications described above, the IRS should notify ICE, USCIS, CBP, the State Department, SSA, banks, lenders, and state and local benefit agencies to prevent downstream benefits from unauthorized work.

Recommendation 13

Leverage Department of Labor Authorities

Although ICE performs investigative and immigration custody duties, effective worksite operations have always required the participation of civil regulators whose mandates intersect with unauthorized employment. The Criminal Investigation Branch of the Internal Revenue Service (IRS-CI), the Office of the Inspector General at the Social Security Administration (SSA/OIG), and the Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate (FDNS) at USCIS all play essential roles. DOL’s enforcement agencies bring the investigative, inspection, and civil-enforcement authorities Congress designed to regulate labor-market conditions.

None of these agencies require arrest authority to inspect employers, interview workers, review records, or enforce the labor-related provisions of the INA. Their civil authorities are not ancillary to worksite enforcement; they are indispensable to it. These authorities are not theoretical; they are active today and formally recognized by DHS.

Various Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs) between DHS and DOL “Concerning Enforcement Activities at Worksites” affirm that DOL possesses independent investigative authority at worksites and may conduct civil enforcement actions alongside or separate from HSI and ERO. DOL’s enforcement agencies already have statutory tools to inspect employers, interview workers, review employment records, and enforce the labor-market protections Congress embedded in the INA. DOL’s own data reinforces why this role matters. According to the National Agricultural Workers Survey, roughly 58 percent of agricultural workers have legal status, a reminder that many assumptions driving public debate about unauthorized labor are not contemporarily accurate.

Moreover, because DHS and DOS effectively represent DOL in the immigration system, when aliens are found to have violated the labor certification ground of inadmissibility at section 212(a)(5)(A) of the INA, DHS must charge them accordingly in removal proceedings. Absent that, the labor-market protections Congress wrote into the statute are never actually enforced.

What has been missing in the coordination of these departments’ duties is not legal authority but rather institutional architecture. No office has been responsible in the past for integrating DOL’s INA-related functions, coordinating them with DHS and DOS, or translating them into a coherent enforcement posture.

DOL’s new Office of Immigration Policy (OIP) exists to close that gap—to unify the authorities DOL already exercises, operationalize them in the present, and build a durable framework for how DOL’s statutory role should function going forward. While DOL evaluates how employment practices affect domestic workers, these functions do not translate into field-level presence or real-time verification of employment authorization. Consequently, DOL’s insights into unauthorized employment arise indirectly through its civil inspections rather than through any immigration-specific mandate. Because of this structural reality, it is essential for OIP to define how DOL’s inspection-derived information should interface with DHS’s immigration and employment-authorization systems, ensuring that DOL’s contributions remain grounded in its civil mission while still informing DHS when unauthorized employment is identified.

Thus, DHS and DOL should revise their current MOUs. Any revised MOU should not be limited to deconfliction, information-sharing, committee structures, or the allocation of responsibilities during joint enforcement operations. The existing MOU and its 2016 Addendum acknowledge DOL’s authorities but fail to specify how those authorities are to be used.

A renewed MOU must articulate what DHS expects from DOL during worksite operations and what DOL can and will provide through its civil inspection and investigative functions. This includes defining the information DOL will collect, procedures for coordinated inspections, the circumstances under which its findings will be shared with DHS, and the respective roles of ICE and DOL’s enforcement agencies when unauthorized employment is discovered. A contemporary MOU would convert long-standing statutory authorities into a predictable operational framework, ensuring each department contributes its mandated functions in a coherent and mutually reinforcing way.

The Wage and Hour Division (WHD) should establish a permanent interagency task force dedicated to worksite enforcement and labor law violations associated with the employment of illegal aliens. This body would mirror the structure of the previous administration’s Child Labor Taskforce, effectively repurposing that model to target workforce exploitation and immigration violations. The task force should include representatives from ICE, USCIS Fraud Detection and National Security (FDNS) division, the DOJ’s Civil Employment Litigation Division, the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC), and willing state regulators.

To extend this cooperation to the local level, the DOL should create an informal version of the 287(g) program for state and local employment law agencies. Through model MOUs, the DOL can formalize the sharing of leads with state Departments of Labor, creating a force multiplier for investigations. Additionally, the Department must institute internal policies to automatically share all potential leads with sister agencies when it lacks the resources to pursue a specific investigation itself, ensuring no violation goes unaddressed.

Congress authorized the DOL to protect domestic workers and regulate labor-market conditions. Currently, however, it has no structured role in assessing whether the large-scale issuance of EADs (employment authorization documents)—particularly to populations whose presence in the labor market is driven solely by economic migration—may adversely affect U.S. workers. USCIS should not grant employment authorization without a clear statutory basis, as it has the practical effect of facilitating further illegal immigration and prolonging unlawful presence by making it easier for aliens to legally earn and remit income than they could through unauthorized work or fraud. At a minimum, though, a renewed MOU between DOL and DHS should include a consultative process in which DOL provides labor-market analysis, sectoral data, and risk assessments to inform DHS’s employment authorization decisions. This would ensure that EAD policy reflects the labor-market protections Congress embedded in the INA, and not simply a desire to minimize the likelihood an alien seeking or who has been granted lawful presence will become a public charge.

Presidential Proclamation (PP) 10,935, “Establishing Project Homecoming,” reinforces the need for a modernized DHS–DOL framework. Section 3(b) in that PP directs DHS to expand its enforcement and removal operations by supplementing its operational force through deputized and contracted personnel. Although PP 10935 does not identify DOL as a source of such personnel, it does direct the DHS secretary to “supplement existing enforcement and removal operations by deputizing and contracting with. . . officers and personnel within other Federal agencies,” which would logically include DOL.

It would be essential, however, for DOL to define the limits of its participation. OIP should ensure DOL’s contributions to Project Homecoming remain grounded in the Department’s civil regulatory mission by clarifying that DOL’s role would be to provide labor-market expertise, inspection-derived information, and regulatory coordination—not to assume direct immigration enforcement authorities. This alignment would preserve the statutory distinction between civil labor authorities and immigration enforcement while ensuring DOL’s functions are integrated coherently into the broader operational environment created by PP 10,935.

The DOL must aggressively utilize the “hot goods” provision of the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) against known violators. This provision empowers the Department to seek court orders preventing the interstate shipment of goods produced in violation of minimum wage or overtime laws. Crucially, these court orders apply to anyone in possession of the tainted goods, not just the original manufacturer. By applying this provision expansively to goods produced by illegal alien labor, the DOL can exert immense economic pressure on entire black market supply chains.

Concurrently, the Department should adopt an internal policy to maximize civil money penalties for all employers found employing illegal aliens. To further strengthen this deterrent, the administration should call on Congress to statutorily increase the caps on civil money penalties for employer violations. Additionally, the process for debarring employer violators from guest worker visa programs must be streamlined and utilized against all eligible violators without exception.

Under the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act (TVPRA), the government has tools to punish peonage, enticement into slavery, sale into involuntary servitude, forced labor, trafficking with respect to peonage, slavery, involuntary servitude, or forced labor, and sex trafficking of children by force, fraud, or coercion. Additionally, the TVPRA requires mandatory restitution for victims of violations and says any venture knowingly benefiting financially from peonage, slavery, or trafficking in persons is equally as liable as the actual traffickers. All of these statutes are routinely violated by employers of trafficking victims, including children like the lost Unaccompanied Alien Children (UAC) of the Biden Administration. The potential penalties for violators are substantial, and strict enforcement against employers knowingly hiring victims of cartel trafficking is required to establish deterrence against dependence on exploited illegal labor. The paltry fines levied on companies found exploiting UACs over the past few years are woefully insufficient as deterrents. The DOL and the DOJ need to closely coordinate investigations and intelligence to ensure all employers operating in violation of the TVPRA are prosecuted and penalized to the fullest extent of the law.

Enforcement resources should be prioritized toward “Low Wage, High Violation” industries, which historically rely heavily on foreign labor and illegal aliens. The DOL should set specific quotas for investigations within these sectors to ensure consistent pressure.

Transparency in reporting is also essential for deterrence. Currently, DOL announcements regarding employer sanctions rarely disclose the immigration status of the workforce involved. Moving forward, all public announcements and reports must identify the immigration status of workers harmed by employer violators. This will accurately reflect the impact of illegal immigration on labor standards.

Recommendation 14

Assign Special Assistant United States Attorneys to Prosecute Immigration-Related Crime

There are many immigration-related criminal offenses in the INA and in Title 18 of the U.S. Code, but most are rarely prosecuted.

In FY 2023, more than 3.2 million aliens were encountered (i.e., apprehended or turned away) by Border Patrol entering or trying to enter illegally, and yet only 5,777 aliens were charged with improper entry under section 275 of the INA that year.

Part of the reason why so few aliens were prosecuted for such straightforward offenses had to do with a lack of interest on the part of the Biden Administration. It should be noted, however, that of the more than 254,000 aliens apprehended by Border Patrol in FY 2025, fewer than 26,000 were charged under section 275. That’s certainly an improvement, but still only represents about ten percent of all border apprehensions.

The threat of criminal prosecution is the most effective deterrent to illegal entry. Many U.S. Attorney’s Offices (USAOs), however, are too busy to file criminal immigration charges, and in most instances, because the penalties for those offenses are minor, such cases are not a high priority for prosecution. That likely explains why more charges (28,854) were filed for felony illegal reentry under section 276 of the INA than for misdemeanor “improper entry” under section 275 of the INA in FY 2025.

Special Assistant United States Attorneys (SAUSAs) are lawyers, often from other federal agencies or local prosecutor’s offices, appointed to assist USAOs in investigating and prosecuting federal cases. DHS should assign lawyers from CBP, USCIS, and ICE OPLA to serve as SAUSAs in every U.S. federal district. That would enable USAOs to prosecute increased numbers of aliens for immigration-related criminal offenses, thus deterring future illegal immigration and increasing the incentives for aliens here illegally to self-deport.

That is especially true given OLC’s June 2025 opinion concluding that “eluding inspection” under section 275(a)(2) of the INA is a continuing offense that can be prosecuted in any federal district in which the alien is found. Millions of aliens across the country are currently subject to prosecution under that provision.

Of the 4,930 aliens charged under section 275 of the INA before federal magistrates in FY 2025, 4,886 (99 percent) were charged in border districts (the Districts of Arizona and New Mexico, the Northern District of New York, and the Southern and Western Districts of Texas).

The appointment of new immigration-trained SAUSAs from DHS in every federal district would increase those totals and expand Section 275 prosecutions nationwide, sending a message to aliens here illegally that the United States is serious about its sovereignty, and that it is better to depart than face the prospect of arrest and incarceration.

Recommendation 15

Reassign Immigration Officers Within DHS

Notwithstanding the additional resources provided in the OBBBA, ICE resources remain limited, but the DHS secretary has the flexibility under the INA to reassign immigration officers to facilitate mass deportation.

According to one source, there are “1,566 state prisons, 98 federal prisons, 3,116 local jails, 1,277 juvenile correctional facilities… and 77 Indian country jails” in the United States, which hold approximately two million individuals altogether.

An untold number of the criminals incarcerated in those facilities are criminal aliens who are removable from the United States, but many of those facilities are remote and ICE ERO lacks the capacity to cover them all.

Taking custody of aliens from criminal detention and confinement is a duty the DHS secretary could assign Border Patrol agents to the degree that CBP has extra capacity. In addition, the secretary could task Border Patrol agents with obtaining criminal conviction records from various courts nationwide that are repositories of those records.

Unless an alien respondent in immigration court admits to a conviction, ICE OPLA attorneys must rely upon properly certified conviction records to sustain criminal removal charges. A failure to provide such records could be fatal to a removal prosecution. To the degree they are available, the secretary of DHS could task Border Patrol agents and CBP officers in OFO with obtaining necessary certified conviction records for removable criminal aliens.

Finally, OFO has a major presence in Hawaii, the only state in the union wholly contained in an island chain. To the degree the office has the capacity, and with the concurrence of appropriate officials, the secretary of DHS should assign CBP officers in OFO to investigate, arrest, and process removable aliens in Hawaii.

Recommendation 16

Place All Interior Immigration Enforcement Operations Inside the Homeland Security Task Force

In section 6 of EO 14159, issued on January 20, 2025, President Trump directed DOJ and DHS to jointly establish Homeland Security Task Forces (HSTFs) in all States nationwide. As the president made clear, those HSTFs were to “include representation from any other Federal agencies with law enforcement officers, or agencies with the ability to provide logistics, intelligence, and operational support to the HSTFs,” as well as representatives “from relevant State and local law enforcement agencies.”

The organizational structure of the HSTF is not a new concept, as its foundation mirrors that of the FBI’s Joint Terrorism Task Forces (JTTFs)—a decentralized network of more than 200 units nationwide, with at least one JTTF located in each of the FBI’s 56 field offices.

Rather than a top-down approach, this network-like model fosters an expansive collaborative environment, leverages localized knowledge and intelligence, and provides operational adaptive and responsive capability, unhindered by bureaucratic decision-making requirements from headquarters. The same should be true of the HSTFs.

The second is “chain of command.” While collaborative, the operational command and oversight of each task force’s mission is clear and unambiguous, with a single lead federal agency. This clarity of oversight reduces territorialism, mission creep, redundant, uncoordinated, independent operations, and wasted resources. The “lead” agencies designation for the HSTFs must be strictly recognized, enforced, and supported at the departmental level and across the administration.

The third has to do with lines of authority and oversight. Although JTTFs are built around a decentralized model, there is a “national level” coordination center, the National Joint Terrorism Task Force (NJTTF), located at FBI Headquarters. The function of the NJTTF is not to run day-to-day operations, but to provide nationwide goals and objectives and a common operating picture, to coordinate information and intelligence, and to allocate funding and requisite resources to the regional task forces. That, too, is a standard for HSTFs to emulate.

Each individual HSTF has four objectives under section 6(c) of EO 14159:

  • Preventing “criminal cartels, foreign gangs, and transnational criminal organizations” from operating in the United States;
  • Dismantling “cross-border human smuggling and trafficking networks;”
  • Ending “the scourge of human smuggling and trafficking, with a particular focus on such offenses involving children;” and
  • Ensuring “all available law enforcement tools” are used “to faithfully execute the immigration laws of the United States.”

The first three objectives flow from the fourth and can only be achieved through faithful execution of our immigration laws. That is why all interior enforcement of the immigration laws should be included within the HSTF model in EO 14159, and why ICE leadership should lead the national HSTF system, with a clear and standardized chain of command in an otherwise decentralized structure.

ERO and HSI each bring their own skills, authorities, and expertise to the task force, and by placing leadership of the national HSTF at the headquarters level of ICE—as is done in the case of JTTFs by FBI—each directorate’s strengths can be best directed toward those four objectives.

Moreover, if interior enforcement is fully housed within the HSTFs, ICE officers and agents will be able to leverage the intelligence and legal authorities of their federal, state, and local law-enforcement partners to ensure that the INA is “faithfully executed.” DHS and DOJ do not need to create a new HSTF structure; the departments already have a model to emulate in the JTTFs.

Recommendation 17

Fully Utilize Other Procedures to Deport Criminal Aliens

Removal proceedings under section 240 of the INA are not the only option for deporting criminal aliens.

Section 238(c) of the INA grants federal district court judges the authority to “enter a judicial order of removal at the time of sentencing against an alien who is deportable, if such an order has been requested by the United States Attorney with the concurrence of” DHS. To obtain a judicial order of removal, the USAO must file a “notice of intent to request judicial removal” with the court “prior to commencement of the trial or entry of a guilty plea,” and then file “a charge containing factual allegations regarding the alienage of the defendant and identifying the crime or crimes which make the defendant deportable under” the criminal grounds of deportability in section 237(a)(2)(A) of the INA “at least 30 days prior to the date set for sentencing.”

Criminal aliens can then claim eligibility for relief under the INA that would allow them to remain in the United States, and if the court finds they have provided “substantial evidence to establish prima facie eligibility for relief from removal under” the act, DHS must “provide the court with a recommendation and report regarding” eligibility for such relief. As in section 240 removal proceedings, the alien must be given “a reasonable opportunity to examine the evidence against him or her, to present evidence on his or her own behalf, and to cross-examine witnesses presented by the Government.”

The benefit to the government of judicial orders of removal is clear: if alien criminals can be ordered removed by district court judges without having to see an IJ, they can be deported as soon as their sentences are completed. The benefit to the alien of such orders can be found in section 238(c)(5) of the INA, which states that the U.S. Attorney, with DHS’s concurrence, may:

“enter into a plea agreement which calls for the alien, who is deportable under this chapter, to waive the right to notice and a hearing under this section, and stipulate to the entry of a judicial order of removal from the United States as a condition of the plea agreement.”

In other words, by accepting a judicial order of removal, the alien can receive a shorter sentence, provided they go back home.

Given that more than 21,000 aliens were federally sentenced in FY 2024 (down from nearly 30,000 in FY 2020, due to lenient Biden-era policies), and 88.7 percent of them were illegal aliens, full implementation of judicial removal orders under section 238(c) of the INA could have a significant impact on annual deportations.

Section 238(a), on the other hand, provides for expedited proceedings for aliens in criminal custody who are deportable because they have been convicted of aggravated felonies or certain drug, firearms, or national security offenses, while they are serving their sentences. That provision is the predicate for the Institutional Hearing and Removal Program (IHRP), which is jointly coordinated by DHS and DOJ and provides for removal hearings (generally conducted via video teleconference) in federal, state, and local facilities.

As DOJ’s Office of the Inspector General reported in September 2021:

“The goal of the IHRP is to issue a final decision on deportation while inmates are still in BOP custody, which typically reduces the time that the IHRP participants spend in ICE detention while awaiting deportation. We found that IHRP participants spent an average of 23 days in ICE detention if they had a final order of deportation prior to release from BOP custody. By contrast, those who did not have a final order when they transferred from BOP custody to ICE detention at the end of their sentence spent an average of 89 days in ICE detention.”

It is unclear how many federal, state, and local facilities participate in the IHRP at present, but DHS, DOJ, and particularly EOIR, should expand that program into every jail, prison, and correctional facility that is willing to accommodate IHRP. Doing so would limit the costs of ICE detention and speed the deportation of criminal aliens.

Finally, the International Prisoner Transfer Program permits “the transfer of prisoners from countries in which they had been convicted and sentenced of crimes to their home countries.” As DOJ explains:

“After transfer, the home or receiving country assumes responsibility for administering the transferred sentence. The transfer program is intended to facilitate the rehabilitation of the transferred offenders and to relieve some of the administration and diplomatic issues that arise with the incarceration of foreign nationals. In addition to foreign national prisoners in federal custody and Americans sentenced abroad, foreign national prisoners in state custody are also eligible to participate in the program.”

The administration should fully expand that program to allow for the transfer of any alien detained on criminal charges in the United States, and DOS should negotiate additional treaties to expand that program.

Recommendation 18

Litigate Challenges Vigorously

District courts, at the urging of alien plaintiffs and immigrants’ advocates, have successfully used temporary restraining orders (TROs) and injunctions to halt deportations.

CRS identified 25 nationwide injunction cases in just the first 100 days of the second Trump Administration, compared to 64 across the entire first Trump term and only 28 during the Biden years.

The most notable early example concerned litigation regarding the Alien Enemies Act (AEA). In March 2025, a D.C. district court judge issued two TROs blocking the removal of Venezuelan nationals, including an order directing that any plane carrying individuals subject to the AEA proclamation that was already en route be returned to the United States. Just over three weeks later, the Supreme Court vacated those TROs, holding that challenges to the AEA must be brought in the district of confinement.

The much more significant challenge the Trump Administration has faced, however, relates to habeas claims filed with federal district courts by aliens in ICE detention seeking release. The Trump Administration has reversed prior interpretations of section 235(b)(2) of the INA and concluded that inadmissible applicants for removal encountered by DHS in the interior of the United States must be detained. The BIA’s opinion in Matter of Yajure Hurtado, affirming that interpretation, has triggered the filing of thousands of habeas petitions under 28 U.S.C. § 2241 in U.S. district courts across the country.

Illegal aliens in detention have fewer incentives to delay their deportations and are more likely to opt for deportation.

In 2025, 28 percent of completed detained removal cases ended with voluntary departure, more than any prior year. The number of aliens in detention is also at a record high, while the percentage of rulings favorable to alien respondents in bond hearings has fallen to 30 percent from 59 percent in 2024.

Despite these developments, habeas petitions have played a significant role in delaying and even preventing the removal of large numbers of illegal aliens. These petitions strain Justice Department resources by forcing DOJ’s Civil Division and the USAOs to respond to each claim.

As noted, the Fifth Circuit has affirmed the BIA’s opinion in Matter of Yajure Hurtado, but it is incumbent on the Justice Department and the Attorney General to secure more such opinions from the other federal courts of appeal, or ideally from the Supreme Court. Moreover, DOJ needs to secure circuit and Supreme Court opinions limiting the authority of trial-level district court judges in review of immigration matters, as Congress plainly intended in section 242 of the INA, along the lines of the Third Circuit’s January opinion in Khalil v. President.

Recommendation 19

Leverage States to Participate

Many state governments possess or are considering laws and orders that reduce incentives for illegal aliens to reside in their states and have proved willing to assist with federal deportation efforts.

Official cooperation efforts between ICE and local law enforcement using the 287(g) program are one of the most effective tools immigration authorities have for collecting large numbers of illegal aliens for deportation. Former ICE Deputy Director Madison Sheahan explained that “These historic partnerships serve as a ‘force multiplier’ to help federal agencies find, arrest, and deport illegal aliens.”

287(g) agreements have increased by 641% since January 2025, but efforts lag in many states. Florida mandates that every sheriff participate in the federal 287(g) program. Thanks to the legislative mandate and coordination by Governor DeSantis’ office, all sixty-seven of Florida’s sheriffs’ departments and seventy-five percent of the state’s law enforcement agencies now have 287(g) agreements; thousands of criminal aliens have already been turned over to ICE. Across every other red state, average participation is only 6.5%.

Initial efforts aimed at identifying the costs illegal aliens impose on states have revealed states can effectively collect and analyze data on illegal alien abuse of the healthcare system. In August 2024, Greg Abbott signed executive order No. GA-46 requiring hospitals to collect data to produce annual reports on the costs of care provided to illegal aliens.

A preliminary report issued by the Texas Health and Human Services Commission (HHSC) on April 25, 2025, found that in November 2024, Texas hospitals incurred $121.8 million in health care costs for persons not lawfully present in the U.S. A similar Florida study found hospitals in that state incurred $659.9 million in losses to provide care for illegal aliens in 2024.

By directing hospitals to collect data on immigration status, these studies reveal precisely where and how much illegal aliens cost American taxpayers. Identity protections prohibit intergovernmental transfer of healthcare data, but insurance and cost studies at the state level generate data that can be used by immigration authorities and lead to targeted regulations on rental, vehicle, and health insurance.

Illegal aliens interact with state agencies frequently as they file taxes, claim benefits, register vehicles, and seek employment. Interagency data sharing has a strong track record of success at the federal level, and while some personal data is protected, state agencies can sign MOUs with ICE to provide non-protected data upon request, rather than requiring a formal court order.

Further action by state legislatures contributes to reducing illegal alien populations and impeding their activities within a state. E-Verify is a federal database used by employers to check the immigration status of its employees.

As of now, seven red states have E-Verify mandates covering all businesses, 12 red states have mandates applying only to public contractors, and 10 additional red states could expand E-Verify coverage through gubernatorial executive order without waiting for legislation or presidential action. Arizona offers a model legislative solution, punishing businesses that refuse to comply with the threat of license revocation and delivering a meaningful reduction in employment of illegal aliens.

The “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” (OBBBA) imposed a 1% remittance tax on certain types of international money transfer. States can add additional taxes on remittances, raising useful funds from the up to $230 billion in remittances sent every year. Oklahoma has taxed remittances to foreign countries for more than a decade. Last year alone, they collected $13 million from just a 1% tax on these transfers. A similar levy in other states will raise revenue while pushing illegal aliens out of the state.

It is time for states to challenge the poorly decided 5–4 Plyler v. Doe Supreme Court case (1982), in which the majority held that barring illegal alien students from public K-12 schools violated the Equal Protection Clause of the 14th Amendment. The U.S. Congress has since legislated on related issues and our immigration system and K-12 public education have changed circumstances. Since 2025, six states (TN, TX, OK, ID, IN, NJ) have introduced legislation that range from collecting immigration status data to charging tuition for illegal alien K-12 students, although none as yet have become law. Given the composition of today’s Court and legal developments emphasizing policymaking restraint from the highest court in the land, a state willing to lead the charge has a good chance of getting Plyler overturned. Willing states could reduce their education costs, preserve resources for American and lawful immigrant students, and encourage illegal aliens with K-12 children to depart at least their states, if not the country.

Success implementing these policies will vary by state, but willing states can play a crucial role in upholding our country’s laws, fighting illegal immigration, and protecting their own citizens, including economically. States can deter illegal aliens from residing in their states by removing benefits that flow from illegal residence in the country and publishing cost data to inform and persuade other states. Especially in states with strong Republican majorities, simple and effective policies supporting immigration enforcement ought to be a tool deployed consistently to support federal immigration policy, including deportations.

Recommendation 20

Track and Publicize Meaningful Benchmarks and Statistics

To achieve one million ICE interior removals in calendar year 2026, the following minimum operational throughput benchmarks should be tracked and reported by the administration on a monthly basis:

Daily case screening volume: the number of deportation cases triaged and referred to the case resolution or apprehension pipeline per day. To screen the existing backlog at the pace required, this number should exceed 5,000 cases per day across all screening personnel, both federal and contracted.

Daily apprehensions: the number of aliens taken into custody by ICE ERO, deputized personnel, and 287(g) partners per day. One million removals in approximately 250 operational days requires an average of 4,000 apprehensions per day, accounting for processing time, legal challenges, and logistical delays between apprehension and actual departure.

Detention bed occupancy and turnover rate: the number of available detention beds, the average daily population, and the average number of days between intake and departure. Faster turnover preserves bed space; slower turnover creates bottlenecks. The administration should target a median detained processing time of no more than 45 days, consistent with historical detained case completion times.

Daily deportation flights and passenger volume: the number of charter and commercial deportation flights per day and the total number of deportees transported. This metric directly measures the output of the entire pipeline and is the most transparent indicator of whether the campaign is on pace.

Self-departure volume: the number of aliens who voluntarily depart through mechanisms such as the CBP Home app, court-granted voluntary departure, or documented exit without government transport. Self-departures are a lagging indicator of enforcement credibility; as apprehension and deportation numbers increase, self-departure should accelerate. This number should be tracked and reported separately from ICE interior removals but recognized as a direct consequence of the enforcement campaign.

These benchmarks are not aspirational. They are the mathematical requirements of achieving one million removals in the time available. The Mass Deportation Coalition’s principle of complete data transparency requires that these numbers be reported publicly and regularly so that the American people, Congress, and the administration itself can assess whether the campaign is on track.

Recommendation 21

Keep HSI Tethered to Immigration Enforcement

The Mass Deportation Coalition is opposed to any separation of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in the appropriations process or organizationally in DHS.

Direct utilization of all internal components of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is essential to maintain a cohesive, seamless collaborative environment in fulfillment of the agency’s statutory mission: “to protect America through criminal investigations and enforcing immigration laws to preserve national security and public safety.”

Cross-border threats posed by transnational criminal organizations constitute an existential threat to the sovereignty, safety, and national security of the United States. These organizations systematically exploit vulnerabilities at our borders and the erosion of immigration law enforcement. Critically, the enforcement of immigration laws and the interdiction of border-related threats are not discrete functions; they are inextricably intertwined, as expressly contemplated by Congress in consolidating investigative, intelligence, and enforcement authorities within ICE under the Homeland Security Act of 2002.

Any proposal to remove or separate, through funding or otherwise, the HSI component from ICE must be summarily rejected as contrary to law and operational necessity. Such further fragmentation of our immigration system would create additional artificial barriers to information sharing and inter-agency collaboration on cross-border criminal matters, thereby undermining HSI’s statutory mandate to investigate violations of the Immigration and Nationality Act, customs laws, and related federal criminal provisions.

The result would be increased bureaucratic delays, wasteful duplication of effort, ambiguous lines of authority, and heightened risks of territorialism and mission creep—precisely the inefficiencies Congress sought to eliminate through the post-9/11 reorganization. This diminution of ICE’s capabilities would materially impair the Department of Homeland Security’s overarching duty to secure the homeland, not enhance it.

Furthermore, any effort to distance HSI from ICE’s immigration enforcement responsibilities would expose the component to political exploitation, advancing extraneous agendas rather than addressing genuine operational requirements. Preservation of the integrated structure is therefore imperative to sustain effective, law-enforcement-driven national security outcomes.

Conclusion — Why We Must Deport

Did America exist before 1776?

The 250th anniversary of our independence is a good time to ask. Answering the question means grappling with the fundamental question underlying the fierce political debates of our time: what exactly it means to be an American.

The answer to that question directs a host of public policies from education to international trade, but none more than immigration. Deciding who comes and why, what’s required of them to stay, and when they must depart stems from some understanding of America.

Not every answer is a good one. Misunderstanding America, confusing it for an economic zone or a multicultural population, has led to decades of destructive immigration policies. These have hurt Americans and eroded our understanding of ourselves. America deserves better.

We, the undersigned representatives of the Mass Deportation Coalition, share a devotion to the nation we call home. This requires us to stand up, speak boldly, and fix the existential crisis that is American immigration. Thanks to President Trump, the urgent need to secure the border has been accomplished. Now is the time for step two: removing the many millions of deportable people in America.

After decades of weak leadership, we finally have a window of opportunity because of President Trump’s clear-eyed understanding of America and the patriotic resolve to make it great again. That window is small. If we do not act—and soon—we will lose our nation. America will cease to mean anything at all.

We the People

If we are to answer the question honestly—did America exist before 1776?—we must first reject the fashionable idea that the nation sprang into existence merely because a group of men signed a document in Philadelphia. Political independence was declared in 1776, but the American people did not suddenly materialize on that summer day. The Declaration announced a nation that already existed in culture, habit, and belief. As Russell Kirk put it, the American order “was not manufactured: rather, it grew.”

Long before independence, a distinct civilization had taken root on this continent. Its institutions, moral assumptions, and public life reflected the inheritance of Western political thought, especially the values of the Old Testament. The settlers who built communities along the Atlantic seaboard did not consider themselves participants in an abstract experiment open to anyone, anywhere, at any time. They were building a society—one with shared norms, obligations, and expectations.

Understanding this is essential to understanding immigration.

A nation is not merely a geographic space or an economic marketplace. It is a people with a shared story and a common inheritance. It possesses borders not only on a map but also in culture, law, and loyalty. When a nation forgets this, it begins to treat citizenship as a commodity rather than an inheritance to be stewarded.

For decades, American immigration policy has operated on precisely that confusion. The United States has often been treated as though it were simply a prosperous territory whose primary purpose is to maximize economic output. In that view, population flows become a labor question. If businesses want cheap labor, the argument goes, immigration should increase accordingly.

But nations are not corporations. Their purpose is not to meet quarterly earnings expectations or return a dividend to a small class of shareholders. Their purpose is the flourishing and continuity of the people who constitute them.

Another misunderstanding has been equally damaging. The popular metaphor of the “melting pot” suggests that America is defined by perpetual cultural transformation, as if the nation were an ever-changing mixture with no stable character at all. In this telling, the only requirement for belonging is the verbal affirmation of a few broad ideals—liberty, equality, opportunity—divorced from the historical context that gave those ideals meaning.

Yet a “creedal nation” that defines itself only by abstract slogans soon finds it lacks the social order necessary to sustain those same ideals. If America is nothing more than a set of universal propositions, then there is no meaningful distinction between citizen and outsider, between membership and mere presence.

History tells a different story. The United States developed within a particular civilizational framework, shaped by institutions, customs, and moral traditions carried across the Atlantic and adapted to new circumstances. Immigration has occurred throughout that history, sometimes at higher levels and sometimes at lower ones, but always in relation to the needs and stability of the nation itself. And always with a mind toward assimilating newcomers to that framework.

Today, however, America faces a challenge that previous generations largely avoided: the weaponization and normalization of mass illegal immigration.

For many years the political class treated the violation of immigration law as a minor inconvenience. Enforcement was inconsistent. Penalties were weak. Public debate focused primarily on economic arguments while ignoring the deeper questions of sovereignty and civic cohesion. The result has been the presence of millions of individuals who entered or remained in the country outside the legal process established by the American people through their laws.

This situation is not merely a bureaucratic problem. It is a constitutional one. A nation that does not enforce its own immigration laws ceases to control one of the most fundamental attributes of sovereignty: determining who may enter and remain within its borders.

The first step toward restoring that sovereignty is securing the border itself. Without physical control of entry, no immigration policy can be credible. The recent success in strengthening border enforcement demonstrates that determined leadership can reverse years of dereliction.

But border security addresses only part of the problem. A nation must also confront the consequences of past failures.

If immigration law is to mean anything, it cannot apply only to those who follow it. Allowing unlawful entry, fraud, and defying departure requirements to become permanent pathways to residence undermine both fairness and legitimacy. This sends a message to the world that the United States lacks the will to enforce the rules it has set for itself.

For this reason, the next phase of immigration enforcement must involve the systematic enforcement of existing law throughout the country. That includes the removal of individuals who entered or remained illegally and those who committed fraud. While such an effort will require significant administrative coordination and political courage, it is neither radical nor unprecedented. Every sovereign nation maintains the authority to remove individuals who reside within its borders unlawfully. And other sovereign nations exercise such authority, unquestioned.

The alternative—permanent acceptance of large-scale illegal presence—is far more radical. It would effectively dissolve the distinction between legal immigration and unlawful entry, rendering the law meaningless and eroding public trust in the institutions meant to uphold it.

None of this implies hostility toward immigrants. Immigration has played an important role in American history, and it may do so again in the future when the nation’s interests require it and when the system can be well-managed. But immigration policy must serve the nation, not replace it.

The United States has reached a moment when clarity is necessary. Either America remains a nation capable of governing its borders and preserving the continuity of its civic life, or it becomes something else entirely: a place defined only by geography and economic opportunity.

The choice before us is therefore not simply about immigration policy. It is about whether America will continue to exist as a nation with a distinct character and a shared destiny.

That question deserves an answer grounded in realism, historical memory, and the courage to act.

This playbook marries the why we must deport with the how. No longer can the cause of mass deportation be considered too operationally or logistically difficult. To the contrary, it is imminently doable, justified, and even necessary. The recommendations in this document chart the path to begin to accomplish a mass deportation campaign, starting with at least one million actual deportations in 2026 so that systems are in place to greatly expand those operations in the years to follow.

The Immigration System

Politicians have long argued for extending amnesty to illegal aliens, even when smaller numbers were historically present in the United States. Today, however, the number of illegal aliens in the United States has grown so large that for many public officials on both sides of the aisle, adopting some form of blanket amnesty policy that would permit most, or even all, aliens here illegally to remain here has become their only proposed “solution” to deal with the catastrophic volume.

As we will show, however, “mass deportation” of millions of aliens here unlawfully is an attainable goal for any administration with the will to carry it out.
