It is a necessary goal that is crucial to maintaining our national security, economic well-being, American identity, and the safety of communities across the United States. These considerations should be at the forefront of this and every future administration’s agenda.

In this playbook, we identify the sources of the government’s authority to deny admission to inadmissible aliens who seek entry and to remove those who are here in violation of law, delineate the statutory grounds that render their presence here unlawful, delineate the authorities Congress has given various government agencies to aid in that deportation effort, clarify how those authorities are used, and most importantly, explain how those authorities can be used to their most impactful effect.

Congress’s Constitutional Authority to Regulate Immigration

All discussions of federal authority begin with the United States Constitution. In the case of immigration enforcement, Article I, Section 8 vests in the Congress the power: “To establish an uniform Rule of Naturalization”; and “To make all Laws which shall be necessary and proper for carrying into Execution the foregoing Powers.”

“Naturalization” is the process by which a foreign national in the United States (defined as an “alien” in section 101(a)(3) of the INA) becomes a “citizen” (as defined by reference therein and in section 101(a)(22) of the INA).

Congress’s power to regulate immigration is therefore a crucial element of its constitutional prerogative “to establish a uniform Rule of Naturalization.” As the nonpartisan Congressional Research Service (CRS) has noted: “Long-standing Supreme Court precedent recognizes Congress as having ‘plenary’ power over immigration, giving it almost complete authority to decide whether foreign nationals (‘aliens,’ under governing statutes and case law) may enter or remain in the United States.”

Supreme Court precedent illustrates this point. In Galvan v. Press, the Court explained:

Policies pertaining to the entry of aliens and their right to remain here are peculiarly concerned with the political conduct of government. In the enforcement of these policies, the Executive Branch of the Government must respect the procedural safeguards of due process. But that the formulation of these policies is entrusted exclusively to Congress has become about as firmly embedded in the legislative and judicial tissues of our body politic as any aspect of our government.

In other words, Congress has the exclusive constitutional authority to write laws controlling immigration, while the Executive Branch has the constitutional obligation to carry out the immigration laws that Congress writes—especially in executing Congress’s decision to preclude the classes of aliens enumerated under section 212(a) of the INA from admission to the United States (collectively known as the “grounds of inadmissibility”).

Section 212(a)(7)(A)(i) of the INA provides the core ground of inadmissibility that Congress created to control the flow of aliens into the United States, barring the admission of any alien “not in possession of a valid unexpired immigrant visa, reentry permit, border crossing identification card, or other valid entry document.”

In addition, section 237(a) of the INA lists the “classes of deportable aliens,” i.e., those aliens who have been admitted to the United States but who, for designated reasons, Congress has directed be removed from the United States.

Those classes include nonimmigrants (i.e., temporary visa holders) who have overstayed their lawful periods of admission or who have otherwise violated the terms of their admission; aliens convicted of certain criminal acts; and aliens who pose a national security risk, an espionage threat, or who expose the nation to the danger of terrorism—both in the United States and abroad.

Key Immigration Enforcement Officials

Section 103(a) charges the Secretary of Homeland Security “with the administration and enforcement of” the INA, subject to certain exceptions.

Subordinates to whom the secretary delegates that enforcement authority are referred to as “immigration officers,” defined in section 101(a)(18) of the INA as “any employee or class of employees of” the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) “or of the United States designated by the” secretary, either “individually or by regulation.”

Among the DHS employees the secretary has designated as immigration officers are:

  • Border Patrol agents in U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP);
  • CBP officers in the agency’s Office of Field Operations (OFO) directorate;
  • U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers in that agency’s Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) directorate;
  • ICE attorneys in the agency’s Office of the Principal Legal Advisor (OPLA);
  • Special agents in the ICE Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) directorate; and
  • U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) asylum officers and refugee officers in the agency’s Refugee, Asylum and International Operations Directorate (RAIO).

CBP has primary jurisdiction over the ports (which are overseen by OFO) and of the borders between the ports (which are under Border Patrol jurisdiction).

ICE ERO has primary jurisdiction for the investigation and arrest of aliens in the interior of the United States, the detention of aliens arrested by ICE and encountered by CBP for civil immigration purposes, and the deportation of aliens from the United States.

Among other duties, ICE HSI is responsible for criminal immigration investigations (including alien smuggling and human trafficking), “worksite enforcement” under section 274A of the INA, and the alien “Student and Exchange Visitor Program” (SEVP).

ICE OPLA attorneys provide legal advice to ICE personnel and represent the interests of the American people in administrative immigration proceedings before the immigration courts and the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA).

Finally, USCIS asylum officers perform “credible fear” and “reasonable fear” screenings and adjudicate “affirmative asylum” applications for aliens in the United States, while refugee officers adjudicate refugee applications abroad.

A provision in section 103(a) of the INA, however, provides that “determination and ruling by the Attorney General”—rather than the Secretary of Homeland Security—“with respect to all questions of law” under the INA “shall be controlling.”

In most instances, the Attorney General delegates this authority to immigration judges (IJs) in the nation’s immigration courts and to the BIA, an administrative review tribunal that reviews immigration decisions, both of which are in the Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR), an agency within the Department of Justice (DOJ).

An IJ is defined in section 101(b)(4) of the INA as “an attorney whom the Attorney General appoints as an administrative judge within” EOIR that has authority to make removal determinations and adjudicate applications for relief for aliens in removal, exclusion, deportation, asylum-only, and withholding-only proceedings; to review negative credible and reasonable fear determinations made by USCIS asylum officers; and to redetermine DHS custody and bond determinations.

With the exception of IJ credible and reasonable fear determinations, the BIA, by regulation, has jurisdiction to review IJ decisions made in those proceedings on appeal and to review USCIS denials of certain visa petitions.

By regulation, the BIA may designate its opinions as “precedents,” meaning they are “binding on” DHS and IJs “in the administration of the immigration laws of the United States,” unless they are “modified or overruled” by a future BIA opinion or by the Attorney General under the regulatory review authority the Attorney General retains under section 103(a).

That precedential authority permits the BIA and Attorney General to change, amend, or clarify immigration policies without going through the conventional regulatory process governed by the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).

Additional exceptions to the DHS secretary’s authority in section 103(a) of the INA relate to “the powers, functions, and duties conferred upon the President, the Attorney General, the Secretary of State, the officers of the Department of State, or diplomatic or consular officers.”

The President as the head of the Executive Branch retains all immigration authority, however, section 212(f) of the INA expressly permits the Chief Executive alone to:

[B]y proclamation, and for such period as he shall deem necessary, suspend the entry of all aliens or any class of aliens as immigrants or nonimmigrants, or impose on the entry of aliens any restrictions he may deem to be appropriate.

In its landmark 2018 decision in Trump v. Hawaii (assessing the legality of travel restrictions imposed by the president on specified aliens from certain countries, which were based on that provision), the Supreme Court concluded that, “[b]y its terms,” section 212(f):

[E]xudes deference to the President in every clause. It entrusts to the President the decisions whether and when to suspend entry (“whenever [he] finds that the entry” of aliens “would be detrimental” to the national interest); whose entry to suspend (“all aliens or any class of aliens”); for how long (“for such period as he shall deem necessary”); and on what conditions (“any restrictions he may deem to be appropriate”).

Finally, section 104 grants the Secretary of State authority over “the administration and the enforcement of” provisions of the INA relating to: “the powers, duties, and functions of diplomatic and consular officers of the United States, except those powers, duties, and functions conferred upon the consular officers relating to the granting or refusal of visas”; and “the determination of nationality of a person not in the United States.”

State Department officers in the Bureau of Consular Affairs (CA) manage the issuance of immigrant and nonimmigrant visas for foreign nationals abroad, while the Secretary sets visa policy.

Subject to exceptions, section 212(a)(3)(C)(i) of the INA also gives the Secretary of State power to exclude an alien if he “has reasonable ground to believe” the alien’s “entry or proposed activities in the United States . . . would have potentially serious adverse foreign policy consequences for the United States.”

Similarly, under section 237(a)(4)(C)(i) of the INA: “An alien whose presence or activities in the United States the Secretary of State has reasonable ground to believe would have potentially serious adverse foreign policy consequences for the United States is deportable.”

Deportability under this provision, however, is subject to the same exceptions that apply to the secretary’s determinations under section 212(a)(3)(C)(i) of the INA.

Other cabinet-level departments also play roles in the enforcement of the immigration laws.

Under section 212(a)(1)(A)(i) of the INA, aliens found to “have a communicable disease of public health significance” under “regulations prescribed by the Secretary of Health and Human Services” (HHS) are inadmissible.

The HHS Secretary is also responsible for the “care and placement” of “unaccompanied alien children” (UACs) encountered by immigration officers with “sponsors” in the United States.

Finally, pursuant to section 212(a)(5)(A)(i) of the INA, aliens seeking to “enter the United States for the purpose of performing skilled or unskilled labor” are inadmissible unless the Secretary of Labor certifies: that there are not enough “workers who are able, willing, qualified . . . and available at the time” those aliens apply for visas “at the place where the alien is to perform such skilled or unskilled labor”; and that the employment of those aliens “will not adversely affect the wages and working conditions of workers in the United States similarly employed.”

“Inspection” and “Admission” of Aliens, and Detention of “Applicants for Admission”

To ensure DHS complies with its “policies pertaining to the entry of aliens,” Congress created a process immigration officers must follow when inspecting aliens who have not been “admitted” to determine whether they should be, which is codified at section 235 of the INA.

The INA defines the term “admitted” as “the lawful entry of the alien into the United States after inspection and authorization by an immigration officer.” Section 235(a)(1) of the INA, in turn, deems all aliens present in this country who have not been admitted—at the ports and borders, and in the interior—as “applicants for admission.”

While CBP officers in OFO perform inspections of applicants for admission at the ports, and Border Patrol inspects aliens encountered at the borders between the ports, ICE ERO officers and HSI special agents inspect unadmitted applicants for admission encountered in the interior.

Pursuant to section 235(b)(2)(A) of the INA, except for aliens subject to “expedited removal” (discussed below), “if the examining immigration officer determines that an alien seeking admission is not clearly and beyond a doubt entitled to be admitted, the alien shall be detained for” removal proceedings before an IJ.

In its September 2025 opinion in Matter of Yajure Hurtado, the BIA found that this detention mandate applies to all unadmitted applicants for admission, including those residing in the interior of the United States.

Thousands of aliens affected by that opinion have filed habeas applications, seeking release from DHS custody pending removal proceedings, and most have been successful.

In February 2026, however, a split panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed the BIA’s conclusions in Matter of Yajure Hurtado, holding that the agency’s current reading of section 235(b)(2)(A) of the INA better reflects Congress’s intent than prior interpretations, which had allowed IJs to release applicants for admission encountered in the interior.

Apprehension and Arrest of Removable Aliens

Even aside from the detention mandates in section 235(b)(2)(A) of the INA, Congress has given immigration officers expansive powers to investigate, question, and detain aliens.

Administrative Arrest Warrants

Section 236(a) of the INA permits immigration officers to issue administrative arrest warrants to take custody of aliens believed to be removable from the United States, pending a decision on whether they are to be removed.

Nothing in the INA requires ICE officers to seek a “judicial warrant” from a federal judge or magistrate before taking an alien into civil custody, regardless of claims to the contrary. Moreover, there is no process immigration officers can follow to obtain a judicial warrant to arrest individual aliens on civil immigration grounds.

Warrantless Questioning and Arrests

Even absent an administrative warrant, section 287(a)(1) of the INA permits immigration officers to “interrogate any alien or person believed to be an alien as to his right to be or to remain in the United States” without a warrant, while section 287(a)(2) allows an immigration officer to “arrest any alien” if the officer has “reason to believe that the alien . . . is in the United States in violation of [the INA or any regulation made pursuant thereto]” and “is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained for his arrest.”

However, section 287(a)(2) also requires immigration officers to take aliens subject to warrantless arrests “without unnecessary delay” for a determination by an examining officer as to whether they have a “right to enter or remain in the United States,” and warrantless immigration arrests require probable cause to believe the subject is a removable alien or has committed a crime.

The leading precedent on civil immigration arrests is INS v. Lopez-Mendoza, a 1984 Supreme Court decision involving two aliens subject to worksite arrests, one in an area agents were permitted by the employer to access, the other in which they were not permitted to enter.

The Court concluded that the “exclusionary rule,” a judicial principle that “prevents the government from using most evidence gathered in violation of the United States Constitution” in criminal cases, does not apply in civil deportation cases.

The purpose of the exclusionary rule, the majority noted, is to deter misconduct by barring the use of improperly obtained evidence, but as the Court held, “several other factors significantly reduce the likely deterrent value of the exclusionary rule in a civil deportation proceeding.”

Specifically, the majority found that “regardless of how the arrest is effected, deportation will still be possible when evidence not derived directly from the arrest is sufficient to support deportation,” given that the primary question in deportation proceedings is the respondent’s identity and alienage.

As the Court noted, the identity of a suspect cannot be suppressed under the exclusionary rule and, as there is no presumption of citizenship under the INA, immigration judges can draw adverse inferences from the respondent’s silence after receiving other proof of alienage.

Finally, as the Court explained, few aliens challenge the lawfulness of their arrests, and therefore, applying the exclusionary rule in civil deportation proceedings likely wouldn’t change agents’ behavior.

Simple Questioning and Brief Detentions

Importantly, the Lopez-Mendoza majority concluded that courts did not need to apply the exclusionary rule in civil deportation proceedings because the then-Immigration and Naturalization Service (INS) had “its own comprehensive scheme for deterring Fourth Amendment violations by its officers.”

ICE replaced the INS in interior immigration enforcement in 2003, and that “comprehensive scheme,” codified at 8 C.F.R. § 287.8, has carried over to the agency’s enforcement operations.

As paragraph (b)(1) therein explains:

Interrogation is questioning designed to elicit specific information. An immigration officer, like any other person, has the right to ask questions of anyone as long as the immigration officer does not restrain the freedom of an individual, not under arrest, to walk away.

Thus, ICE officers require no proof of either alienage or criminality to question individuals in public, unless those individuals questioned reasonably believe they are free not to respond or leave.

ICE officers only need suspicion of alienage or criminality when the subject does not feel free to walk away from questioning, but as 8 C.F.R. § 287.8(b)(2) explains:

If the immigration officer has a reasonable suspicion, based on specific articulable facts, that the person being questioned is, or is attempting to be, engaged in an offense against the United States or is an alien illegally in the United States, the immigration officer may briefly detain the person for questioning.

In the criminal context, such detentions are referred to as “Terry stops” after the Supreme Court’s 1969 opinion in Terry v. Ohio, which established that “reasonable suspicion” standard.

More specifically, the Court there explained that “in justifying the particular intrusion, the police officer must be able to point to specific and articulable facts which, taken together with rational inferences from those facts, reasonably warrant that intrusion.”

“Probable Cause” for Immigration Arrests

Under limitations in 8 C.F.R. § 287.8(c)(2), however, immigration officers can only perform a warrantless arrest under section 287(a)(2) of the INA “when the designated immigration officer has reason to believe that the person to be arrested has committed an offense against the United States or is an alien illegally in the United States.”

As CRS has explained, “reviewing courts have interpreted the ‘reason to believe’ standard for warrantless immigration arrests” under section 287(a)(2) of the INA (and by extension, the regulation) as “equivalent to the Fourth Amendment’s probable cause standard.”

CRS continues:

Under this [probable cause] standard, courts have held that an immigration officer must have sufficient facts that would lead a reasonable person to believe, based on the circumstances, that the alien has violated federal immigration laws and is likely to escape before an ICE warrant can be obtained.

Detention Under the Immigration and Nationality Act

Detention of aliens subject to removal proceedings is mandatory under various provisions of the INA, both (as noted) for inadmissible “applicants for admission” as defined in section 235(a)(1), and for certain aliens subject to deportability and who are under final orders of removal.

Expedited Removal and the Detention Mandates in Section 235(b) of the INA

Again, under section 235(a)(1) of the INA, an alien who arrives at a port of entry or between the ports, or is present in the United States, but who has not been admitted is deemed “an applicant for admission” and is subject to inspection under section 235(a)(3) of the INA.

If, following that inspection, the immigration officer determines an applicant for admission lacks required admission documents (and thus inadmissible under section 212(a)(7)(A)(i) of the INA) or is seeking admission via fraud (and therefore inadmissible under section 212(a)(6)(C) of the INA) the officer has two different statutory options for processing the alien.

Section 235(b)(1)(A)(i) of the INA allows the officer to “order the alien removed…without further hearing or review”—i.e., without obtaining a removal order from an IJ under section 240 of the INA—“unless the alien indicates either an intention to apply for asylum . . . or a fear of persecution.” This process is known as “expedited removal.”

Under section 235(b)(1)(A)(ii) of the INA, however, if an alien subject to expedited removal requests asylum or claims a fear of persecution if returned, the immigration officer must “refer the alien for an interview by” a USCIS asylum officer to determine whether that alien has a “credible fear of persecution.”

“Credible fear of persecution” is defined as “a significant possibility, taking into account the credibility of the statements made by the alien in support of the alien’s claim and such other facts as are known to the officer, that the alien could establish eligibility for asylum under” section 208 of the INA.

Accordingly, “credible fear” is a screening standard to determine whether an alien may be eligible for asylum.

Congress is clear, however, in section 235(b)(1)(B)(iii)(IV) of the INA, that aliens “shall be detained pending a final determination of credible fear of persecution and, if found not to have such a fear, until removed.”

Section 235(b)(1)(B)(ii) of the INA is equally clear that if an asylum officer “determines at the time of the interview that an alien has a credible fear of persecution . . ., the alien shall be detained for further consideration of the application for asylum.”

Detention is critical in this context to the credibility of the inspection process because the credible fear standard is low, and asylum is particularly susceptible to fraud. As the House explained at the time it was drafting what would become the expedited removal provision:

Existing procedures to deny entry to and to remove illegal aliens from the United States are cumbersome and duplicative. Removal of aliens who enter the United States illegally, even those who are ordered deported after a full due process hearing, is an all-too-rare event. The asylum system has been abused by those who seek to use it as a means of “backdoor” immigration.

Alternatively, immigration officers performing inspections may process applicants for admission who are inadmissible under sections 212(a)(7)(A)(i) or 212(a)(6)(C) of the INA using the same procedures Congress mandated for aliens inadmissible under the remaining grounds of inadmissibility, by placing them directly into section 240 removal proceedings, under section 235(b)(2)(A) of the INA.

As with aliens subject to expedited removal, aliens processed under section 235(b)(2)(A) of the INA and who are not “clearly and beyond a doubt entitled to be admitted” must “be detained.”

The only process for releasing an inadmissible applicant for admission pending removal proceedings is on “parole” under section 212(d)(5)(A) of the INA.

That provision states, in pertinent part, that the DHS secretary:

[M]ay, in his discretion parole into the United States temporarily under such conditions as he may prescribe only on a case-by-case basis for urgent humanitarian reasons or significant public benefit any alien applying for admission to the United States, but such parole of such alien shall not be regarded as an admission of the alien and when the purposes of such parole shall, in the opinion of the [DHS Secretary], have been served the alien shall forthwith return or be returned to the custody from which he was paroled and thereafter his case shall continue to be dealt with in the same manner as that of any other applicant for admission to the United States.

The congressional limitations on DHS’s authority are apparent from the highlighted portions of that statute.

First, parole may only be granted “on a case-by-case basis,” and thus may not be issued on a blanket basis to allow the entry of large numbers of aliens, or programmatically.

Second, DHS may only grant parole for either “urgent humanitarian reasons” or “significant public benefit.” Granting parole for any other purpose is thus ultra vires, as it exceeds the scope of statutory parole authority.

Third, an alien granted parole is not “admitted” to the United States, and therefore, legally, remains in the same immigration status he or she held when parole was granted.

Fourth, the DHS secretary may revoke parole at any time in the secretary’s unreviewable discretion, if the secretary is satisfied that the “purposes of such parole . . . have been served,” after which the paroled alien must return or be returned to DHS custody.

Note that in section 3(d) of the Laken Riley Act, Congress gave standing to state attorneys general to seek injunctive relief to enforce the restrictions on parole in section 212(d)(5) of the INA. To date, no actions have been filed against the Trump Administration under that provision.

Detention under Section 236(a) and Release of Aliens Arrested on Warrant

As noted, section 236(a) of the INA authorizes immigration officers to arrest and detain an alien on an administrative warrant “pending a decision on whether the alien is to be removed from the United States.”

Section 236(a) of the INA further permits DHS to continue to detain aliens arrested on warrant or release them on a bond of not less than $1,500 or conditional parole, which is distinct from parole under section 212(d)(5)(A) of the INA.

By regulation, with exceptions, aliens detained by DHS under section 236(a) can request release either from the department or, alternatively, from IJs in bond proceedings, which are “separate and apart” from removal proceedings under section 240 of the INA.

Neither section 236(a) of the INA nor the applicable regulations, however, confer on an alien any right to release on bond.

Instead, an alien in DHS detention seeking an IJ bond redetermination under section 236(a) “must establish to the satisfaction of the Immigration Judge . . . that he or she does not present a danger to persons or property, is not a threat to the national security, and does not pose a risk of flight.”

Conversely, DHS does not bear the burden of showing that the alien should be detained.

Mandatory Detention Under Sections 236(c) and 242(a)(2) of the INA

As with the congressional restrictions on DHS’s authority to release inadmissible applicants for admission under section 235(b) of the INA, the act bars other aliens from seeking release from civil immigration custody.

For example, section 241(a)(1) of the INA requires DHS to remove aliens under final orders of removal within 90 days, designated in statute as the “removal period.”

Section 241(a)(2) of the INA, in turn, directs the department to detain those aliens during the removal period, and makes clear that “[u]nder no circumstance during the removal period shall” DHS “release an alien who has been found” removable under the criminal and national-security grounds of inadmissibility and deportability.

Similarly, section 236(c) of the INA requires DHS to “take into custody any alien” who:

  • Is inadmissible under the criminal grounds of inadmissibility in section 212(a)(2) of the INA;
  • Is removable under the “terrorist activities” grounds of inadmissibility and deportability in sections 212(a)(3)(B) and 237(a)(4)(B) of the INA (respectively);
  • Is deportable under certain criminal grounds of deportability in section 237(a)(2) of the INA; or
  • “Is charged with, is arrested for, is convicted of, admits having committed, or admits committing acts which constitute the essential elements of any burglary, theft, larceny, shoplifting, or assault of a law enforcement officer offense, or any crime that results in death or serious bodily injury to another person.”

That last class of criminal aliens subject to mandatory detention was added to section 236(c) of the INA by the Laken Riley Act.

In addition, the Laken Riley Act gives standing to state attorneys general to sue for injunctive relief to force DHS to detain:

  • Inadmissible applicants for admission at the borders and ports subject to mandatory detention under section 235(b) of the INA;
  • Other aliens subject to mandatory detention under section 236(c) of the INA; and
  • Aliens ordered removed pending deportation under section 241(a)(2) of the INA (criminal aliens in particular).

DHS must take those criminal aliens described in section 236(c) of the INA, as amended by the Laken Riley Act, into its custody “when the alien is released” from incarceration, “without regard to whether the alien is released on parole, supervised release, or probation, and without regard to whether the alien may be arrested or imprisoned again for the same offense.”

The detention mandate in section 236(c) was added to the INA by section 303 of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 (IIRAIRA). As the House explained in its 1996 Report on an earlier iteration of the IIRAIRA, “a chief reason why many deportable aliens are not removed from the United States is the inability of the INS to detain such aliens through the course of their deportation proceedings,” underscoring the crucial role of detention in immigration enforcement.

Removal Proceedings

With exceptions below, DHS must obtain a final removal order from an IJ or the BIA before it can deport a removable alien from the United States.

Prior to the commencement of removal proceedings, DHS must serve an alien charged with removability a “Notice to Appear” (NTA), which (inter alia) must explain the nature of the proceedings, list the acts the alien is alleged to have committed that are in violation of law, and provide the specific grounds of removability and the time and place of the first removal hearing (known colloquially as the “initial Master calendar”).

Commencement of Proceedings

Removal proceedings commence when DHS files the NTA with the immigration court.

The alien (denominated the “respondent” in immigration proceedings) is thereafter required to appear before an IJ at the initial Master calendar hearing.

Unless reset for counsel, the IJ will then explain the respondent’s rights in those proceedings and the charges and describe the nature of the proceedings.

If the alien is unrepresented, the IJ must provide a list of free or low-cost legal service providers and provide the alien opportunity to find counsel (unless the alien waives counsel and elects to proceed pro se). If the alien is unable to proceed in English, the court will also provide an interpreter.

While respondents have “the privilege of being represented” in immigration court and before the BIA, section 292 of the INA makes clear such representation must be “at no expense to the Government,” meaning the alien must either hire an attorney or secure pro bono legal counsel if the alien wants representation.

Once those steps are completed, the IJ will place the respondent under oath and require the alien to plead to the allegations in the NTA.

“Relief”

Most respondents admit the allegations in the NTA and concede removability to move to the next stage of the removal proceedings, where the alien will seek “relief,” that is, some benefit or protection that, if granted, will permit the respondent to remain in the United States.

Asylum is the form of relief most respondents seek in removal proceedings. Of the nearly 3.8 million pending cases in the current immigration court backlog, more than 2.4 million (63.3 percent) involve a pending asylum application.

“In Absentia” Removals

Unless their presence is waived, respondents must appear at each of their immigration court removal hearings.

If the respondent receives notice of the hearing and fails to appear, however, and the alien has conceded removability or ICE counsel can otherwise establish the alien is removable, the IJ must order the alien removed in absentia.

In FY 2025, IJs issued roughly 485,500 removal orders, more than 306,500 of which were issued in absentia (63 percent of the total) because the alien failed to appear in immigration court.

Aliens ordered removed in absentia are ineligible for a period of 10 years for most discretionary forms of relief except for asylum.

The respondent has 180 days after the issuance of an in absentia removal order to move the court to reopen the case, either because the alien’s “failure to appear was because of exceptional circumstances,” or because the respondent did not receive notice of the hearing.

The filing of a motion to reopen will stay the IJ’s in absentia removal order, however, no hearing notice is required if the respondent failed to file a change of address with the immigration court.

BIA Appeals

After the IJ has issued a final order, either an order of removal or granting relief, both the respondent and ICE may file an appeal with the BIA.

Under current regulations, all appeals must be filed with the Board within 30 days from the date the IJ issued the decision, and either party may file a brief on appeal.

Petitions for Review

After the BIA has issued its opinion, the alien may file a petition for review with the U.S. court of appeals “in which the immigration judge completed the proceedings.”

Under the “‘zipper’ clause” in section 242(b)(9) of the INA, trial-level federal district courts have little, if any, jurisdiction over decisions made in removal hearings, despite efforts by district court judges to intervene in cases pending before the immigration courts.

Deportation

Aliens under final orders of removal have received their full due process rights and must depart the United States or be deported.

Despite that fact, acting ICE Director Todd Lyons recently revealed that the agency is “‘tracking’” 1.6 million aliens subject to final deportation orders in this country, 800,000 of whom also have criminal convictions.

The “Removal Period”

As noted, section 241(a)(1) of the INA requires DHS to remove aliens under final orders of removal within 90 days, designated in statute as the “[r]emoval period,” and section 241(a)(2) of the INA requires the department to detain those aliens during the removal period.

Few of those aliens are taken into custody and detained, however. Instead, ICE ERO generally sends the alien a “Notice to Deportable Alien to Surrender” (Form I-166), a Form I-205, “Warrant of Removal”, and a Form I-294, “Warning to Alien Ordered Removed or Deported,” informing the alien to report at a time and place certain for removal.

The Form I-166 is also called a “bag and baggage letter” but is commonly referred to as a “run letter” because it informs aliens under final orders that ICE is looking for them.

As explained below, admitted aliens charged with deportability under section 237(a) of the INA who are under final removal orders face criminal penalties, including imprisonment pursuant to section 243(a)(1) of the INA if they fail to depart within 90 days of the issuance of such orders, but enforcement of that provision is rare.

There is no similar sanction for aliens charged with inadmissibility under section 212(a) of the INA who are under final removal orders but who fail to depart.

“Recalcitrant” Countries

One major impediment to many deportations is the refusal of so-called “recalcitrant” countries to provide necessary travel documents for their nationals.

As ICE has explained:

As part of the removal process, the U.S. government requests that foreign governments take appropriate steps to confirm the citizenship of individuals suspected to be their nationals—including conducting interviews when necessary; the timely issuance of travel documents, where appropriate; and the acceptance of the physical return of their nationals by scheduled commercial flights or, where necessary, special charter flights.

Any lack of cooperation from the nation of origin delays, and in many cases, inhibits the removal process. Countries classified by ICE as uncooperative are also known as recalcitrant. Factors that could lead to a country being classified as recalcitrant include hindering ICE removal efforts by refusing to take the appropriate steps, as described above.

Other Immigration Proceedings

While removal proceedings under section 240 of the INA are the most common proceedings at which an alien’s removability is assessed, they are not the only one.

Expedited Removal

As explained above, section 235(b)(1) of the INA permits immigration officers to issue legally binding “expedited removal” orders without referring inadmissible applicants for admission to removal proceedings before an immigration judge.

“Asylum-Only” Proceedings

The “visa-waiver program” (VWP), authorized under section 217 of the INA, permits nationals of 41 countries to travel to the United States as visitors for pleasure or business for stays of 90 days or less without first obtaining a B-1 or B-2 nonimmigrant visa.

Under section 217(b) of the INA, however, OFO may not grant nationals of those countries a visa waiver unless those aliens also waive: (1) any challenges to their admissibility, and (2) their right “to contest, other than on the basis of an application for asylum, any action for removal.”

If VWP aliens violate the terms of their admission (most commonly by overstaying their authorized periods of admission), they are not entitled to removal hearings under section 240 of the INA. The only forms of relief available to them are humanitarian protections, which they can seek in “asylum-only” proceedings.

VWP aliens are not the only class of respondents who are subject to asylum-only proceedings. “Stowaways” found to have a credible fear of removal, nonimmigrants under the D (crewmen landing temporarily) and S (informants) categories, and aliens subject to removal on security grounds may also be placed in asylum-only proceedings.

“Withholding-Only” Proceedings

Finally, aliens who reenter illegally after formal removal and aliens in expedited removal proceedings under section 238 of the INA due to aggravated felony convictions who claim a fear of harm if returned may only seek two humanitarian protections in “withholding-only” proceedings: (1) “statutory withholding” of removal; and protection under Article III of the Convention Against Torture (CAT).

As DOJ explains: “Neither party may raise any other issues including issues of admissibility, deportability, eligibility for waivers, and eligibility for any other form of relief from removal,” (including asylum) in withholding-only proceedings—the sole issue is whether the respondent has established eligibility for statutory withholding of removal or CAT.

“Unlawful Employment of Aliens”

Not all civil immigration enforcement involves the arrest, detention, prosecution, and deportation of removable aliens.

Under section 274A(a)(1)(A) of the INA, it is “unlawful for a person or other entity to hire, or to recruit or refer for a fee, for employment in the United States an alien” if the employer knows the employee “is an unauthorized alien with respect to such employment.”

Similarly, section 274A(a)(2) of the INA makes it unlawful for employers “to continue to employ [an] alien in the United States knowing the alien is (or has become) an unauthorized alien with respect to such employment.”

Known as the “employer sanctions” provisions of the INA, Section 274A provides both civil and criminal penalties for employers who violate the requirements therein. ICE policing of those requirements is referred to as “worksite enforcement.”

The “Employment Verification System”

The “[e]mployment verification system” in section 274A(b) of the INA requires U.S. employers to verify the employment eligibility of their new workers and to certify on the “Form I-9 Employment Eligibility Verification Form” that they have examined documents presented by those workers which establish their eligibility to be employed in the United States.

New employees must also attest on the Form I-9 that they are authorized to work in this country, and employers are required to retain those forms for set periods and present them to ICE, DOJ, or DOL upon request.

ICE Investigations

To ensure employers are complying with section 274A of the INA, ICE HSI performs “worksite enforcement investigations,” which commence with service on the employer of a “Notice of Inspection” (NOI).

By regulation, employers have three business days after receipt of the NOI to provide HSI with its Forms I-9 and any “supporting documentation”—including “a copy of the employer’s payroll, a list of active and terminated employees, articles of incorporation, and business licenses”—requested in the notice.

At the end of the inspection process, ICE HSI provides the employer with the results of its investigation by serving the employer with either a “Compliance Letter,” a “Notice of Suspect Documents,” a “Notice of Discrepancies,” a “Notice of Technical or Procedural Failures,” or a “Warning Notice.”

Notices of Suspect Documents also advise employers of “the possible criminal and civil penalties for continuing to employ unauthorized aliens” and provide employers and suspect employees with “an opportunity to provide documentation demonstrating valid U.S. work authorization if they believe the finding is in error.”

Administrative Proceedings

If the ICE worksite inspection uncovers substantive violations of the verification process, uncorrected paperwork failures, or “knowing hire” or “continuing to employ” violations, ICE may issue the employer a “Notice of Intent to Fine” (NIF) specifying the violations alleged and the amount of any proposed fine.

Employers can request a hearing within 30 days of service of the NIF before an Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) in EOIR’s Office of the Chief Administrative Hearing Officer (OCAHO), but in most instances ICE reaches an agreement with those employers on the fine and any necessary compliance measures prior to ICE OPLA filing a complaint.

By regulation, penalties for knowingly hiring an illegal alien can range from between $275 (for a first offense prior to March 27, 2008) to $28,619 for a third offense or subsequent involving a hire after November 2, 2015.

“Paperwork” fines for violations of the Form I-9 process run from between $100 to $2,861 per violation.

DOJ, on behalf of DHS, may also bring a civil action in federal district court pursuant to section 274A “requesting relief, including a permanent or temporary injunction, restraining order, or other order against the person or entity” as the Attorney General “deems necessary.”

Criminal Proceedings

Under section 274A(f) of the INA, employers may also face criminal penalties for a “pattern or practice of violations” for knowingly hiring illegal aliens for employment.

Fines of up to $3,000 for such violations may be imposed “for each unauthorized alien with respect to whom such a violation occurs,” and employers may also be “imprisoned for not more than six months for the entire pattern or practice.”

Criminal Violations of the Immigration and Nationality Act

In addition to civil deportation and removal penalties, aliens and others may also face criminal penalties for violations of the INA.

“Bringing in and Harboring Certain Aliens”

Section 274(a)(1)(A) of the INA makes it unlawful:

  • To bring a known alien to the United States at any place other than a designated port of entry;
  • To knowingly or recklessly transport or move an alien who has come to, entered, or remains in this country in violation of law within the United States;
  • To knowingly or recklessly conceal, harbor, or shield from detection any alien present in violation of law; and
  • To encourage or induce an alien to come to, enter, or reside in the United States, knowing or in reckless disregard of the fact that such coming to, entry, or residence is or will be in violation of law.

In addition, attempts to bring aliens into the United States illegally, move or transport illegal aliens in this country, or conceal, harbor, or shield them from detection are also criminal acts, as are conspiracies to commit any offense under section 274(a)(1)(A) of the INA, or any act that aids or abets in the commission of those offenses.

Penalties can include imprisonment and/or a fine.

“Improper Entry by Alien”

Aliens face criminal punishment for three separate but related violations under section 275(a) of the INA:

  1. Entering or attempting to enter “at any time or place other than as designated by immigration officers;”
  2. “Elud[ing] examination or inspection by immigration officers;” or
  3. Entering or attempting to enter the United States “by a willfully false or misleading representation or the willful concealment of a material fact.”

Violations of those provisions are misdemeanors subject to imprisonment of up to 6 months and a fine for a first offense and felonies with possible punishment of up to 2 years’ incarceration and a fine for a second or subsequent offense.

Illegal entry under section 275(a)(1) of the INA is a “completed” offense at the time the alien crosses illegally, meaning that the alien must be prosecuted in the federal district where the alien entered; but in June 2025, the Office of Legal Counsel (OLC) at DOJ issued an opinion concluding that “eluding” inspection under section 275(a)(2) “is a continuing offense” for purposes of venue.

As noted above, aliens present in the United States who have not been admitted are deemed “applicants for admission” under section 235(a)(1) of the INA, and as OLC explained:

It would make no sense to impose a criminal sanction on an alien who “eludes” that necessary inspection at a port of entry while sparing another alien, whom immigration officials are just as responsible for inspecting, of that same sanction merely because he “eludes” his inspection somewhere else.

Accordingly, eluding inspection under section 275(a)(2) is an ongoing violation that continues until the alien is encountered by DHS, and violators may be prosecuted in any federal district in which that encounter occurs.

“Reentry of Removed Aliens”

Under section 276(a) of the INA, any alien “who has been denied admission, excluded, deported, or removed or has departed the United States while an order of exclusion, deportation, or removal is outstanding” and who reenters, attempts to reenter, or “is at any time found in, the United States” without permission from DHS has committed a felony, subject at a minimum to a fine and imprisonment of up to 2 years.

Harsher penalties apply for aliens who were previously removed after convictions for certain crimes or on national security grounds, including up to 20 years for aliens convicted of “aggravated felonies.”

Violation of the Alien Registration Provisions

With exceptions, section 262 of the INA requires aliens “now or hereafter in the United States” who are 14 years of age or older and have “not been registered and fingerprinted” under specified provisions of the law, and who remain in the United States for 30 or more days, to “apply for registration and to be fingerprinted before the expiration of such 30 days.”

Parents and guardians are required to register on behalf of their children.

Nonetheless, for decades prior to the second Trump Administration, the INS and its successor agencies in DHS only required legal aliens who had been vetted and complied with the visa-issuance and admissions processes to register—not aliens here unlawfully or who had overstayed their nonimmigrant visas.

That began to change, however, on January 20, 2025, when President Trump issued Executive Order (EO) 14159, entitled “Protecting the American People Against Invasion.”

Section 7 of that EO, “Identification of Unregistered Illegal Aliens,” directed the DHS Secretary, in coordination with the State Department and DOJ, to: “immediately announce and publicize information about the legal obligation of all previously unregistered aliens in the United States to comply with” the INA registration requirements; “ensure that all previously unregistered aliens in the United States comply with” those requirements; and “ensure that failure to comply with” those “legal obligations . . . is treated as a civil and criminal enforcement priority.”

In accordance with EO 14159, the DHS Secretary announced in February 2025 that DHS would begin enforcing the INA registration requirements, “to track illegal aliens and compel them to leave the country voluntarily.”

USCIS thereafter set up an “Alien Registration Requirement” web page with a link to the new Form G-325R, “Biographic Information (Registration),” which aliens can complete to register online.

On March 12, 2025, DHS published an interim final rule (IFR) with these new requirements (to take effect a month later) and inviting public comments on them.

Immigrants’ advocates challenged the new rule in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia in late March 2025, but the D.D.C. denied their motion to prevent the requirements from taking effect, concluding the plaintiffs lacked standing to bring the case.

On August 12, 2025, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit denied the plaintiffs’ request for a stay or injunction of that decision pending appeal. The registration requirement is now in effect.

As USCIS explains, aliens who have registered under that program must “carry . . . and have in their personal possession evidence of registration,” a requirement that stems from section 264(e) of the INA.

Registered aliens must also provide the agency with a change of address within 10 days of moving within the United States, as required by section 265(a) of the INA.

Section 266 of the INA provides criminal penalties for aliens who fail to comply with DHS’s new “registration” and “change of address” mandates.

A willful failure to register may subject an alien to a fine of up to $1,000 and/or imprisonment of up to 6 months (a misdemeanor), while an alien’s failure to provide a change of address is also a misdemeanor carrying a possible fine of up to $200 and/or imprisonment for up to 30 days.

An alien’s failure to carry proof of registration is again a misdemeanor, with a possible sentence of 30 days’ incarceration and/or a fine of up to $100 upon conviction.

“Failure to Depart”

Pursuant to section 243(a) of the INA, it is a felony for an alien ordered removed under section 237(a) after admission to willfully fail or refuse to depart from this country within 90 days.

In addition, it is a crime for an alien under a final removal order based on charges under section 237(a) to willfully fail or refuse to apply for “travel or other documents necessary to the alien’s departure,” to “connive or conspire” to “prevent or hamper or with the purpose of preventing or hampering the alien’s departure,” or to willfully fail or refuse to appear for removal.

Violation of any of these provisions exposes the offender to imprisonment upon conviction for up to four years and a fine, though there are exceptions, and the court may suspend these penalties in certain instances.

Appendix B

Creatively Employ a Whole-of-Government Effort

The scale of the illegal alien presence in the United States demands creative, out-of-the-box ideas. Options that may run into legal and administrative issues cannot be dismissed without evaluation. The fact remains that the illegal population dwarfs the size of government agencies intended to arrest and deport them. Many policy thinkers have suggested using the military for a mass deportation operation. This consideration is not without historical precedent, as the Eisenhower Administration considered the same before ultimately deciding to use military-tactics and former personnel at the then-Immigration and Naturalization Services.

A deportation campaign operating at the scale the Trump Administration has pursued requires coordination across federal departments, the military, the Justice Department, and in the private sector. No single agency possesses the manpower, facilities, transportation assets, or legal resources to remove millions of people within a compressed political timeline. The operational challenge is not primarily one of authority but of capacity, and meeting it demands a deliberate fusion of institutional capabilities that do not ordinarily operate in concert.

DHS: The Legal and Operational Backbone

The Department of Homeland Security provides the legal and operational backbone. ICE ERO and CBP’s processing infrastructure establish the chain of custody, deportation order pipeline, and biometric collection systems. But current staffing cannot sustain removals at the volume the administration demands.

At-large arrests increased by 600 percent in the first nine months of 2025, with officers drawn from agencies as varied as the FBI and the IRS surging into the field.

Supplementing federal ranks with contracted personnel may offer temporary surge capacity that would avoid permanent headcount growth. Notably, private firms like Deployed Resources, which initially built camps for music festivals, has secured contracts to erect and operate tent detention facilities at military bases.

Department of Defense Contributions

The Department of Defense could contribute physical infrastructure and personnel. Executive Order 14,167 assigned U.S. Northern Command (USNORTHCOM) the mission of sealing the borders and deterring unlawful mass migration, narcotics trafficking, and human smuggling.

The administration has deployed over 10,000 members of the armed services to border operations, tripling the force present on Inauguration Day.

Military installations offer controlled perimeters, existing airfields, and life-support capacity that commercial facilities cannot match. DHS has asked DOD to help detain immigrants on bases nationwide, with Fort Bliss designated as a central hub capable of holding up to 10,000 people and serving as a model for potentially ten additional facilities.

Congressional Funding

Litigation units must scale in parallel. Congress passed an unprecedented $170 billion spending package for immigration enforcement through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, including $45 billion explicitly for expanding civil immigration detention. Without legal resources that match operational tempo, the adjudication process would become a chokepoint for removals.

Aviation and Ground Transportation

Commercial aviation and ground transportation could round out the contractor contribution.

In 2025, there were an estimated 2,202 immigration enforcement removal flights. For February 2026, the ICE Flight Monitor tracked at least 1,630 flights.

DHS also signed a contract worth nearly $140 million to purchase six Boeing 737s, enabling ICE to operate its own fleet.

It’s worth further emphasizing that current deportation flight resources are insufficient to support a mass deportation campaign. The ICE Flight Monitor tracked approximately 1,393 enforcement flights in a single month at peak, averaging 45 flights per day. Even assuming full loads on narrow-body aircraft, this effort would fall well short of the daily deportation volume required to achieve one million removals in 2026. The six Boeing 737s DHS has contracted to purchase will supplement but not resolve this shortfall. A mass deportation campaign requires the allocation of flight resources operating at a fundamentally different scale.

Widebody Charter Aircraft Fleet

DHS could contract for a fleet of widebody charter aircraft sufficient to transport deportees to their countries of origin at the daily volume the campaign requires. One million removals over the approximately 250 operational days remaining in 2026 would require an average daily volume of 4,000 deportations, accounting for weekends, maintenance cycles, and logistical variability. A fleet of widebody aircraft, each carrying between 300 and 400 passengers, operating multiple rotations per day to high-volume destination countries, can achieve this goal.

The charter fleet could be procured through a contracted transportation provider with demonstrated experience in nonstandard aviation operations, government air charter, and high-security passenger transport. The contracting entity would be required to provide flight crews, aircraft maintenance, and qualified in-flight security personnel for each deportation flight. In-flight security is a nonnegotiable requirement; the safe transport of deported aliens on international flights would require trained security teams with protocols for managing noncompliant individuals at altitude.

Charter flights could depart primarily from military installations with adequate runway infrastructure, as described above. This would collocate detention, processing, and departure functions on the same federal facility, minimizing ground transportation requirements and eliminating the security risks associated with moving deportees through commercial airports and across public roadways. For destination countries in Central America, the Caribbean, and northern South America, departure points along the Gulf Coast and southern border would be optimal. For deportees returning to countries in Africa, South Asia, or East Asia, departure points at installations with long-range aerial port capacity on the East and West Coasts could be designated.

As at present, the charter air component could be supplemented by commercial air carriers for deportees whose countries of origin are served by direct commercial routes and who present lower security risks. Commercial carrier agreements are less expensive per seat than charter operations but are subject to scheduling constraints and carrier willingness. For high-volume corridors (particularly Mexico, Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador), dedicated charter operations would be more reliable and scalable than commercial alternatives.

And, as at present, ground transportation between detention facilities and departure points could be managed by contracted transportation teams using a fleet of secure buses and vehicles procured or leased for the duration of the campaign. The ground transportation network connects the tiered detention system (local jails, IGA facilities, military installation camps) to the charter departure points, completing the end-to-end logistics chain from apprehension to repatriation.

The Integrated Whole-of-Government Model

The result would be a model where DHS provides authority, DOD provides infrastructure and additional resources, the ICE OPLA and DOJ would provide legal finality, and contractors could provide the manpower and transport that surge capacity demands. Each institution would contribute what it does best, and the contractor layer would dissolve when the mission concludes.

Achieving one million interior removals in 2026 requires operational resources that exceed the current capacity of any single federal agency. ICE ERO, even with the additional resources provided by the OBBBA, would be hard pressed to generate the case screening, apprehension, detention management, and transportation volume necessary to meet this target using existing and planned federal personnel alone. The operational model, however, could incorporate a contracted surge workforce that operates under federal authority, supplements existing agency capacity, and ends when the mission is completed, leaving no permanent headcount or long-term benefit obligations on the federal payroll.

This contracted pipeline could be organized into six functional phases, each staffed by a dedicated team operating under the direction and legal authority of DHS:

Phase 1 – Case Screening

A contracted legal screening team of lawyers and paralegals could supplement existing ICE OPLA, DOJ, and CBP legal resources to triage all deportation cases. The screening function would serve as the intake for the entire pipeline. Each case would be reviewed to determine whether a given alien has a pending deportation order, receives or is dependent on public benefits, is ineligible for asylum, or presents a security threat.

Cases involving removable aliens should be prioritized in the following order:

  1. Security threats and violent criminals with existing deportation orders;
  2. Security threats without pending orders;
  3. Individuals who receive or are dependent upon public benefits; and
  4. All other aliens residing in violation of immigration law.

Cases involving aliens with existing final orders should bypass screening and flow directly to the locate and apprehension phases.

Phase 2 – Case Resolution

A contracted litigation team should supplement government counsel to handle court filings and manage legal challenges at the volume required. Current litigation resources are insufficient to process cases at the scale this campaign demands. The contracted litigation team would operate in close coordination with ICE OPLA and DOJ and utilize automated court filing systems and mass hearing dockets to accelerate case resolution.

ICE OPLA should ensure that aliens who fail to appear at scheduled hearings receive in absentia deportation orders, and those aliens should be immediately referred to the apprehension pipeline. The contracted litigation team should be composed of attorneys and paralegals capable of managing high caseloads in a standardized process that allows for rapid analysis and processing without sacrificing legal sufficiency.

Phase 3 – Locate Deportees

A contracted skip tracing team could use government records, arrest records, financial data, and open-source intelligence to locate aliens with deportation orders. Identifying information for those who cannot be located should be entered into NCIC as discussed elsewhere in this playbook, increasing the likelihood that any subsequent contact with state or local law enforcement would trigger a detention and transfer.

Aliens currently housed in government-sponsored accommodations should be among the first targeted, as their residence in such facilities is itself evidence of receipt of means-tested public benefits.

Phase 4 – Apprehend Deportees

The most critical element of the contracted surge would be the apprehension workforce. Contracted personnel cannot independently exercise law enforcement authority; they must be deputized under federal authority to make lawful arrests. Presidential Proclamation 10,935, “Establishing Project Homecoming,” directs the DHS Secretary to “supplement existing enforcement and removal operations by deputizing and contracting with officers and personnel within other Federal agencies.” The same legal framework could potentially extend to qualified contracted personnel who are deputized as federal law enforcement officers for the duration of the mass deportation campaign.

The deputization pipeline could draw from retired ICE ERO officers; retired CBP agents; retired special agents from HSI, FBI, DEA, ATF, and the U.S. Marshals Service; retired state and local law enforcement officers; and qualified military veterans with relevant operational backgrounds. While additional screening would be necessary, such individuals should possess the training, judgment, and operational temperament required for interior enforcement operations.

A properly structured contracted training program could convert these experienced professionals into deputized enforcement officers through an accelerated curriculum focused on immigration law authorities, arrest and detention procedures under sections 236(a) and 287(a) of the INA, Fourth Amendment standards for probable cause and Terry stops, use of force policy, and interagency coordination protocols.

Once trained, equipped, and deployed, all deputized personnel would fall under the operational control of the DHS chain of command through the Homeland Security Task Force structure described elsewhere in this playbook. The contracting entity would handle administrative functions: payroll, benefits, travel, lodging, and equipment procurement. All operational tasking, targeting, and field direction would remain with DHS leadership. Such a division of responsibilities would mirror the model used successfully in other federal surge operations, in which contracted personnel have supplemented organic government capacity under career governmental authority and direction.

Phase 5 – Detain and Process Deportees

Contracted personnel could manage the daily operations of detention and out-processing facilities, including those erected on military installations as described below. Contracted detention staff could process deportees for removal, collect biometric data for ICE/CBP databases, coordinate with foreign governments to obtain repatriation clearances, and file final disposition reports. The contracted detention workforce would supplement, but not replace, federal detention management. ICE ERO would retain authority over custody determinations and release decisions.

Phase 6 – Transportation

As at present, contracted transportation teams could manage the movement of deportees from detention facilities to ports of departure, including both ground transportation to embarkation points and charter air operations for international repatriation flights.

Three Governing Principles

Three principles should govern any contracted surge model:

First, temporality: The contracted workforce exists for the duration of the mass deportation campaign and dissolves when the mission concludes. The government would accept or accrue no long-term salary, pension, or benefit obligations. This would be a surge capacity model, not a permanent expansion of the federal workforce.

Second, federal authority: No contracted personnel could or should exercise independent enforcement authority. All arrests, detentions, and removals must occur under the legal authority of DHS through deputization, delegation, or direct supervision. The contracting entity would provide manpower, equipment, and administrative support. The government would provide legal authority, operational direction, and command.

Third, accountability: The contracting entity must be subject to rigorous oversight, including regular reporting through the DHS hierarchy, and comply with all applicable use-of-force policies and data transparency requirements consistent with the Mass Deportation Coalition’s principles on meaningful metrics. The contracted workforce should not be a means of circumventing oversight; it should be a means of achieving operational scale while maintaining the legal and procedural standards that give the deportation campaign its legitimacy.

Poll Results

National Survey of 1,000 Likely Voters conducted by McLaughlin & Associates for the Immigration Accountability Project, March 2026.

Economic Issues and Immigration Importance

Three in five (62%) are economic issue voters with inflation/cost of living (41%) as the dominant single issue. Immigration/border increases in importance among those who approve of Trump (22%), Trump voters (17%), and Republicans (17%). Although affordability dominates, addressing illegal immigration is an important priority to nearly three-quarters (72%), including 42% who say it is “very” important.

Trump Voters: Motivation and GOTV Opportunity

In the 2024 presidential election, 4 in 5 (82%) Trump voters were more likely to vote for Donald Trump because of his promise to conduct the largest mass deportation operation in American history. Trump voters universally support (87%) the President exceeding the previous largest deportation effort led by President Eisenhower. If President Trump exceeds one million deportations of illegal migrants in 2026, three-quarters (74%) of Trump voters would be more likely to vote for the Republican candidate for Congress.

Majority Consensus on Immigration Principles

Four in five (82% to 13%) agree that immigration policy should serve the interests of American citizens. Over three-quarters (78% to 18%) believe immigration to the United States is a privilege, not a right, and America has the right to decide who may enter our country. Three-quarters (76% to 20%) agree that the first duty of the American government is to protect American citizens, not illegal aliens. The majority (52% to 40%) sees a problem: they believe the federal government has put the interests of illegal immigrants above the interests of poor Americans, including veterans and the elderly.

Partisan Divides When Politicized

Three-quarters (76% to 20%) agree with President Trump’s SOTU statement that the first duty of the American government is to protect American citizens, not illegal aliens. The majority (52%) “strongly” agrees. Under half (46%) are less likely to vote for a Democrat who refused to stand up when President asked members to stand in support of the statement. When the statement is politicized, it can be divisive — this can motivate and energize Trump voters (76%) and Republicans (75%).

Majority Consensus on Illegal Immigration Law & Order

Four in five (80% to 15%) believe America has an obligation to enforce the immigration laws Congress enacts. Over three-quarters (77% to 18%) agree businesses that repeatedly violate immigration hiring laws should face escalating penalties. Nearly three-quarters (73% to 19%) believe all federal agencies should cooperate in the enforcement of immigration laws. Over two-thirds agree on three law-and-order statements: state governments should share information on illegal migrants with the federal government (68% to 24%); protesters who attack or harass law enforcement officers while they are enforcing the laws passed by Congress should be arrested and prosecuted (67% to 26%); and failure to enforce immigration laws places additional strain on local schools, hospitals, welfare services, and first responders (67% to 20%).

Two-Thirds Support Fundamental Deportation Policies

Two-thirds (66% to 27%) support deporting migrants who enter the country illegally. Two in five (41%) “strongly” support it. Two-thirds (66% to 27%) support immediately deporting the 1.6 million illegal migrants who have been issued final deportation orders. Two-thirds (65% to 28%) support deporting foreign tourists and other temporary visitors who remain in the country past the expiration date of their travel visas.

Broad Majority Support for Workplace Illegal Immigration Policies

Over two-thirds, ranging from 69% up to 82% support illegal immigration policies in the workplace. Workplace policies are extremely popular among Trump voters and Republicans. There is bipartisan support among two-thirds of Independents and the majority of Democrats. Support is stronger among White voters, but the majority of Hispanics favor the policies.

Voters Oppose Exploitation of Illegal Migrant Labor

Three-quarters of voters believe big corporations should not be allowed to benefit from cheaper illegal migrant labor, when that labor is subsidized by American taxpayers. Four in five voters consider it unfair for the wealthy to benefit from illegal migrant labor while the working class has to compete against illegal migrant labor. Eliminating migrant worker exploitation by increasing automation and mechanization of farms and factories is divisive.

Broad Support to Deport Illegal Migrants Who Rely on Taxpayer Funded Welfare

By a 3 to 1 ratio, the vast majority of voters support deporting illegal migrants in the United States who rely on taxpayer-funded welfare benefits. Roughly half of voters "strongly" support it.

Majority Opposes Illegal Migrants Having Access to U.S. Financial System

The majority of voters oppose illegal migrants having access to our financial system, including banks. Three in five voters support increasing the 1% tax on money transfers made by illegal migrants and applying the tax to all money transfers sending money back to their home counties.
